If the r-by-r submatrix is a principal submatrix, then its determinant is a principal minor (of size r); ifthe submatrix is a leading principal matrix, then its determinant is a leading principal minor; if the submatrix is a trailing principal submatrix, then its determinant is a trailing principal minor. By convention, the empty principal minor is 1; that is, det $A [ \emptyset ] = 1$ 

A signed minor, such as those appearing in the Laplace expansion (0.3.1.1) $[ ( - 1 ) ^ { i + j }$ det $A _ { i j } ]$ is called a cofactor; if we wish to indicate the size of the submatrix, we call its signed determinant a cofactor ofsize r. 

0.7.2 Partitions, block matrices, and multiplication. If $\alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { t }$ constitute a partition of $\{ 1 , \ldots , m \}$ and $\beta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \beta _ { s }$ constitute a partition of $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , then the matrices $A \left[ \alpha _ { i } , \beta _ { j } \right]$ form a partition of the matrix $A \in M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } ) , 1 \leq i \leq t , 1 \leq j \leq s$ If $A \in M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ and $B \in M _ { n , p } ( \mathbf { F } )$ are partitioned so that the two partitions of $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ coincide, the two matrix partitions are said to be conformal. In this event, 

$$
(A B) \left[ \alpha_ {i}, \gamma_ {j} \right] = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {s} A \left[ \alpha_ {i}, \beta_ {k} \right] B \left[ \beta_ {k}, \gamma_ {j} \right]\tag{0.7.2.1}
$$

in which the respective collections of submatrices $A [ \alpha _ { i } , \beta _ { k } ]$ and $B [ \beta _ { k } , \gamma _ { j } ]$ are conformal partitions of A and B, respectively. The left-hand side of (0.7.2.1) is a submatrix of the product AB (calculated in the usual way), and each summand on the righthand side is a standard matrix product. Thus, multiplication of conformally partitioned matrices mimics usual matrix multiplication. The sum of two partitioned matrices A, $B \in M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ of the same size has a similarly pleasant representation if the partitions of their rows (respectively, of their columns) are the same: 

$$
(A + B) \left[ \alpha_ {i}, \beta_ {j} \right] = A \left[ \alpha_ {i}, \beta_ {j} \right] + B \left[ \alpha_ {i}, \beta_ {j} \right]
$$

If a matrix is partitioned by sequential partitions of its rows and columns, the resulting partitioned matrix is called a block matrix. For example, if the rows and columns of $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ are partitioned by the same sequential partition $\alpha _ { 1 } = \{ 1 , \ldots , k \} , \alpha _ { 2 } =$ $\{ k + 1 , \ldots , n \}$ , the resulting block matrix is 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A [ \alpha_ {1}, \alpha_ {1} ] & A [ \alpha_ {1}, \alpha_ {2} ] \\ A [ \alpha_ {2}, \alpha_ {1} ] & A [ \alpha_ {2}, \alpha_ {2} ] \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} & A _ {1 2} \\ A _ {2 1} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

in which the blocks are $A _ { i j } = A [ \alpha _ { i } , \alpha _ { j } ]$ . Computations with block matrices are employed throughout the book; $2 { \cdot } \mathrm { b y } { - } 2$ block matrices are the most important and useful. 

0.7.3 The inverse of a partitioned matrix. It can be useful to know the corresponding blocks in the inverse of a partitioned nonsingular matrix A, that is, to present the inverse of a partitioned matrix in conformally partitioned form. This may be done in a variety of apparently different, but equivalent, ways — assuming that certain submatrices of $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ and $A ^ { - 1 }$ are also nonsingular. For simplicity, let A be partitioned as a 2-by-2 block matrix 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} & A _ {1 2} \\ A _ {2 1} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

with $A _ { i i } \in M _ { n _ { i } } ( \mathbf { F } ) , i = 1 , 2$ , and $n _ { 1 } + n _ { 2 } = n$ . A useful expression for the correspondingly partitioned presentation of $A ^ { - 1 }$ is 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c c} \left(A _ {1 1} - A _ {1 2} A _ {2 2} ^ {- 1} A _ {2 1}\right) ^ {- 1} & A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2} \left(A _ {2 1} A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2} - A _ {2 2}\right) ^ {- 1} \\ A _ {2 2} ^ {- 1} A _ {2 1} \left(A _ {1 2} A _ {2 2} ^ {- 1} A _ {2 1} - A _ {1 1}\right) ^ {- 1} & \left(A _ {2 2} - A _ {2 1} A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2}\right) ^ {- 1} \end{array} \right]\tag{0.7.3.1}
$$

assuming that all the relevant inverses exist. This expression for $A ^ { - 1 }$ may be verified by doing a partitioned multiplication by A and then simplifying. In general index set notation, we may write 

$$
A ^ {- 1} [ \alpha ] = \left(A [ \alpha ] - A [ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} ] A [ \alpha^ {c} ] ^ {- 1} A [ \alpha^ {c}, \alpha ]\right) ^ {- 1}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{c} A ^ {- 1} \left[ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} \right] = A \left[ \alpha \right] ^ {- 1} A \left[ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} \right] \left(A \left[ \alpha^ {c}, \alpha \right] A \left[ \alpha \right] ^ {- 1} A \left[ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} \right] - A \left[ \alpha^ {c} \right]\right) ^ {- 1} \\ = \left(A \left[ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} \right] A \left[ \alpha^ {c} \right] ^ {- 1} A \left[ \alpha^ {c}, \alpha \right] - A \left[ \alpha \right]\right) ^ {- 1} A \left[ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} \right] A \left[ \alpha^ {c} \right] ^ {- 1} \end{array}
$$

again assuming that the relevant inverses exist. There is an intimate relationship between these representations and the Schur complement; see (0.8.5). Notice that $A ^ { - 1 } [ \alpha ]$ is a submatrix of $A ^ { - 1 }$ , while $A [ \alpha ] ^ { - 1 }$ is the inverse of a submatrix of A; these two objects are not, in general, the same. 

0.7.4 The Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury formula. Suppose that a nonsingular matrix $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ has a known inverse $A ^ { - 1 }$ and consider $B = A + X R Y$ , in which X is n-by-r, Y is $r { \mathrm { - } } \mathbf { b y } { \mathrm { - } } n .$ , and R is r-by-r and nonsingular. If B and $R ^ { - 1 } + Y A ^ { - 1 } X$ are nonsingular, then 

$$
B ^ {- 1} = A ^ {- 1} - A ^ {- 1} X (R ^ {- 1} + Y A ^ {- 1} X) ^ {- 1} Y A ^ {- 1}\tag{0.7.4.1}
$$

If r is much smaller than n, then R and $R ^ { - 1 } + Y A ^ { - 1 } X$ may be much easier to invert than B. For example, if $x , y \in \mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ are nonzero vectors, $X = x , Y = y ^ { T } , y ^ { T } A ^ { - 1 } x \neq - 1$ and $R = [ 1 ]$ , then (0.7.4.1) becomes a formula for the inverse of a rank-1 adjustment to A: 

$$
\left(A + x y ^ {T}\right) ^ {- 1} = A ^ {- 1} - \left(1 + y ^ {T} A ^ {- 1} x\right) ^ {- 1} A ^ {- 1} x y ^ {T} A ^ {- 1}\tag{0.7.4.2}
$$

In particular, if $B = I + x y ^ { T }$ for $x , y \in \mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ and $y ^ { T } x \neq - 1$ , then $B ^ { - 1 } = I - ( 1 +$ $y ^ { T } x ) ^ { - 1 } x y ^ { T }$ 

0.7.5 Complementary nullities. Suppose that $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is nonsingular, let α and $\beta$ be nonempty subsets of $\left\{ 1 , \ldots , n \right\}$ , and write $| { \boldsymbol { \alpha } } | = r$ and $| \beta | = s$ for the cardinalities of α and $\beta$ . The law of complementary nullities is 

$$
\text { nullity } (A [ \alpha , \beta ]) = \text { nullity } \left(A ^ {- 1} \left[ \beta^ {c}, \alpha^ {c} \right]\right)\tag{0.7.5.1}
$$

which is equivalent to the rank identity 

$$
\operatorname{rank} (A [ \alpha , \beta ]) = \operatorname{rank} \left(A ^ {- 1} \left[ \beta^ {c}, \alpha^ {c} \right]\right) + r + s - n\tag{0.7.5.2}
$$

Since we can permute rows and columns to place first the r rows indexed by α and the s columns indexed by $\beta _ { ; }$ , it suffices to consider the presentations 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} & A _ {1 2} \\ A _ {2 1} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right] \text {   and   } A ^ {- 1} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} B _ {1 1} & B _ {1 2} \\ B _ {2 1} & B _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

in which $A _ { 1 1 }$ and $B _ { 1 1 } ^ { T }$ are $r { \mathrm { - } } { \mathsf { b y } } { \mathrm { - } } s$ and $A _ { 2 2 }$ and $B _ { 2 2 } ^ { T }$ are $( n - r ) –  { \mathbf { b } }  { \mathbf { y } } – ( n - s )$ . Then (0.7.5.1) says that nullity $A _ { 1 1 } = \mathrm { n u l l i t y } B _ { 2 2 }$ 

The underlying principle here is very simple. Suppose that the nullity of $A _ { 1 1 }$ is k. If $k \geq 1$ , let the columns of $X \in M _ { s , k } ( \mathbf { F } )$ be a basis for the null space of $A _ { 1 1 }$ . Since A is nonsingular, 

$$
A \left[ \begin{array}{c} X \\ 0 \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} A _ {1 1} X \\ A _ {2 1} X \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ A _ {2 1} X \end{array} \right]
$$

has full rank, so $A _ { 2 1 } X$ has k independent columns. But 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{c} B _ {1 2} (A _ {2 1} X) \\ B _ {2 2} (A _ {2 1} X) \end{array} \right] = A ^ {- 1} \left[ \begin{array}{c} 0 \\ A _ {2 1} X \end{array} \right] = A ^ {- 1} A \left[ \begin{array}{c} X \\ 0 \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c} X \\ 0 \end{array} \right]
$$

so $B _ { 2 2 } ( A _ { 2 1 } X ) = 0$ and hence nullity $B _ { 2 2 } \geq k = \mathrm { n u l l i t y }$ $A _ { 1 1 }$ , a statement that is trivially correct if $k = 0$ . A similar argument starting with $B _ { 2 2 }$ shows that nullity $A _ { 1 1 } \geq$ nullity $B _ { 2 2 }$ . For a different approach, see (3.5.P13). 

Of course, (0.7.5.1) also tells us that nullity $A _ { 1 2 } = \mathrm { n u l l i t y } B _ { 1 2 }$ , nullity $A _ { 2 1 } =$ nullity $B _ { 2 1 }$ , and nullity $A _ { 2 2 } =$ nullity $B _ { 1 1 } . \mathrm { I f } r + s = n$ , then rank $A _ { 1 1 } = \operatorname { r a n k } B _ { 2 2 }$ and rank $A _ { 2 2 } = \mathrm { r a n k } B _ { 1 1 }$ , while if $n = 2 r = 2 s$ , then we also have rank $A _ { 1 2 } = \mathrm { r a n k } B _ { 1 2 }$ and rank $A _ { 2 1 } = \operatorname { r a n k } B _ { 2 1 }$ . Finally, (0.7.5.2) tells us that the rank of an r-by-s submatrix of an n-by-n nonsingular matrix is at least $r + s - n$ 

0.7.6 Rank in a partitioned matrix and rank-principal matrices. Partition $A \in$ $M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ as 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} & A _ {1 2} \\ A _ {2 1} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right], \quad A _ {1 1} \in M _ {r} (\mathbf {F}), \mathbf {A} _ {2 2} \in M _ {n - r} (\mathbf {F})
$$

If $A _ { 1 1 }$ is nonsingular, then of course rank $\left[ A _ { 1 1 } \quad A _ { 1 2 } \right] = r$ and rank ${ \left[ \begin{array} { l } { A _ { 1 1 } } \\ { A _ { 2 1 } } \end{array} \right] } = r$ . Remarkably, the converse is true: 

$$
\text { if   } \operatorname{rank} A = \operatorname{rank} [ A _ {1 1} A _ {1 2} ] = \operatorname{rank} \left[ \begin{array}{c} A _ {1 1} \\ A _ {2 1} \end{array} \right], \text {   then   } A _ {1 1} \text {   is   nonsingular }\tag{0.7.6.1}
$$

This follows from $_ { ( 0 . 4 . 6 ( \mathrm { c } ) ) }$ : If $A _ { 1 1 }$ is singular, then rank $A _ { 1 1 } = k < r$ , and there are nonsingular S, $T \in M _ { r } ( \mathbf { F } )$ such that 

$$
S A _ {1 1} T = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} I _ {k} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 _ {r - k} \end{array} \right]
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\hat {A} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} S & 0 \\ 0 & I _ {n - r} \end{array} \right] A \left[ \begin{array}{c c} T & 0 \\ 0 & I _ {n - r} \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} I _ {k} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 _ {r - k} \end{array} \right] & S A _ {1 2} \\ A _ {2 1} T & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

has rank r, as do its first block row and column. Because the rth row of the first block column of $\hat { A }$ is zero, there must be some column in $S A _ { 1 2 }$ whose rth entry is not zero, which means that $\hat { A }$ has at least $r + 1$ independent columns. This contradicts rank $\hat { A } =$ rank $A = r$ , so $A _ { 1 1 }$ must be nonsingular. 

Let $A \in M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ and suppose that rank $A = r > 0$ . Let $A = X Y ^ { T }$ be a fullrank factorization with $X , Y \in M _ { m , r } ( \mathbf { F } )$ ; see (0.4.6c). Let α, $\beta \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , m \}$ and $\gamma , \delta \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , n \}$ be index sets ofcardinality r. Then $A [ \alpha , \gamma ] = X [ \alpha , \varnothing ^ { c } ] Y [ \gamma , \varnothing ^ { c } ] ^ { T } \in$ $M _ { r } ( { \bf F } )$ , which is nonsingular whenever rank $X [ \alpha , \mathcal { D } ^ { c } ] = \operatorname { r a n k } Y [ \gamma , \mathcal { D } ^ { c } ] = r$ . The multiplicativity property (0.3.5) ensures that 

$$
\det A [ \alpha , \gamma ] \det A [ \beta , \delta ] = \det A [ \alpha , \delta ] \det A [ \beta , \gamma ]\tag{0.7.6.2}
$$

Suppose that $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ and rank $A = r$ . We say that A is rank principal if it has a nonsingular r-by-r principal submatrix. It follows from (0.7.6.1) that if there is some index set $\alpha \subset \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ such that 

$$
\operatorname{rank} A = \operatorname{rank} A [ \alpha , \varnothing^ {c} ] = \operatorname{rank} A [ \varnothing^ {c}, \alpha ]\tag{0.7.6.3}
$$

(that is, if there are r linearly independent rows of A such that the corresponding r columns are linearly independent), then A is rank principal; moreover, $A [ \alpha ]$ is nonsingular. 

If $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is symmetric or skew symmetric, or if $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { C } )$ is Hermitian or skew Hermitian, then rank $A \left[ \alpha , \mathcal { O } ^ { c } \right] = \operatorname { r a n k } A \left[ \mathcal { O } ^ { c } \right]$ , α] for every index set $\alpha .$ so A satisfies (0.7.6.3) and is therefore rank principal. 

0.7.7 Commutativity, anticommutativity, and block diagonal matrices. Two matrices A, $B \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ are said to commute if $A B = B A$ . Commutativity is not typical, but one important instance is encountered frequently. Suppose that $\Lambda = [ \Lambda _ { i j } ] _ { i , i = 1 } ^ { s } \in$ $M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is a block matrix in which $\Lambda _ { i j } = 0$ if $i \neq j ; \Lambda _ { i i } = \lambda _ { i } I _ { n _ { i } }$ for some $\lambda _ { i } \in \mathbf { F }$ for each $i = 1 , \dots , s ;$ ; and $\lambda _ { i } \neq \lambda _ { j }$ if i $\neq j$ . Partition $B = [ B _ { i j } ] _ { i , j = 1 } ^ { s } \in M _ { n } ( { \bf F } )$ conformally with . Then $\Lambda B = B \Lambda$ if and only if $\lambda _ { i } B _ { i j } = B _ { i j } \lambda _ { j }$ for each $i , j = 1 , \dots , s$ , that is, $( \lambda _ { i } - \lambda _ { j } ) B _ { i j } = 0$ for each $i , j = 1 , \dots , s$ . These identities are satisfied if and only if $B _ { i j } = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$ . Thus,  commutes with B ifand only if B is block diagonal conformal with ; see (0.9.2). 

Two matrices $A , B \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ are said to anticommute if $A B = - B A$ . For example, the matrices $\left[ { \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { - 1 } \end{array} } \right]$ and $\left[ { \begin{array} { c c } { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 1 } & { 0 } \end{array} } \right]$ anticommute. 

0.7.8 The vec mapping. Partition a matrix $A \in M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ according to its columns: $A = [ a _ { 1 } \dots a _ { n } ]$ . The mapping vec : $M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } ) \to \mathbf { F } ^ { m n }$ is 

$$
\operatorname{vec} A = [ a _ {1} ^ {T} \dots a _ {n} ^ {T} ] ^ {T}
$$

that is, vec A is the vector obtained by stacking the columns of A, left to right. The vec operator can be a convenient tool in problems involving matrix equations. 

## 0.8 Determinants again

Some additional facts about and identities for the determinant are useful for reference. 

0.8.1 Compound matrices. Let $A \in M _ { m , n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ . Let $\alpha \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , m \}$ and $\beta \subseteq$ $\{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ be index sets of cardinality $r \leq \mathrm { m i n } \{ m , n \}$ elements. The $\binom { m } { r } -  { \mathbf { b } }  { \mathbf { y } } - \binom { n } { r }$ matrix whose $\alpha , \beta$ , entry is det $A [ \alpha , \beta ]$    is called the rth compound matrix of A and is denoted by $C _ { r } ( A )$ . In forming the rows and column of $C _ { r } ( A )$ , we arrange index sets lexicographically, that is, {1, 2, 4} before {1, 2, 5} before {1, 3, 4}, and so on. For example, if 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 1 0 \end{array} \right]\tag{0.8.1.0}
$$

then $C _ { 2 } ( A ) =$ 

$$
\left[ \begin{array}{l l l} \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 5 \end{array} \right] & \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & 6 \end{array} \right] & \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 6 \end{array} \right] \\ \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & 2 \\ 7 & 8 \end{array} \right] & \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 1 & 3 \\ 7 & 1 0 \end{array} \right] & \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 2 & 3 \\ 8 & 1 0 \end{array} \right] \\ \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 4 & 5 \\ 7 & 8 \end{array} \right] & \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 4 & 6 \\ 7 & 1 0 \end{array} \right] & \det \left[ \begin{array}{l l} 5 & 6 \\ 8 & 1 0 \end{array} \right] \end{array} \right] = \left[ \begin{array}{r r r} - 3 & - 6 & - 3 \\ - 6 & - 1 1 & - 4 \\ - 3 & - 2 & 2 \end{array} \right]
$$

If $A \in M _ { m , k } ( \mathbf { F } ) , B \in M _ { k , n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ , and $r \leq \operatorname* { m i n } \{ m , k , n \}$ , it follows from the Cauchy–Binet formula (0.8.7) that 

$$
C _ {r} (A B) = C _ {r} (A) C _ {r} (B)\tag{0.8.1.1}
$$

which is the multiplicativity property of the rth compound matrix. 

We define $C _ { 0 } ( A ) = 1$ . We have $C _ { 1 } ( A ) = A ; { \mathrm { i f ~ } } A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ , then $C _ { n } ( A ) = \operatorname* { d e t } A$ 

$$
\text {   If   } A \in M _ {m, k} (\mathbf {F}) \text {   and   } t \in \mathbf {F}, \text {   then   } C _ {r} (t A) = t ^ {r} C _ {r} (A)
$$

$$
\text {   If   } 1 \leq r \leq n, \text {   then   } C _ {r} (I _ {n}) = I _ {\binom {n} {r}} \in M _ {\binom {n} {r}}
$$

$$
\text {   If   } A \in M _ {n} \text {   is   nonsingular   and   } 1 \leq r \leq n, \text {   then   } C _ {r} (A) ^ {- 1} = C _ {r} (A ^ {- 1})
$$

$$
\text {   If   } A \in M _ {n} \text {   and   } 1 \leq r \leq n, \text {   then   } \det C _ {r} (A) = (\det A) ^ {\binom {n - 1} {r - 1}}
$$

$$
\text {   If   } A \in M _ {m, n} (\mathbf {F}) \text {   and   } r = \operatorname{rank} A, \text {   then   } \operatorname{rank} C _ {r} (A) = 1
$$

$$
\text {   If   } A \in M _ {m, n} (\mathbf {F}) \text {   and   } 1 \leq r \leq \min \{m, n \}, \text {   then   } C _ {r} (A ^ {T}) = C _ {r} (A) ^ {T}
$$

$$
\text {   If   } A \in M _ {m, n} (\mathbf {C}) \text {   and   } 1 \leq r \leq \min \{m, n \}, \text {   then   } C _ {r} (A ^ {*}) = C _ {r} (A) ^ {*}
$$

If $\Delta = [ d _ { i j } ] \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is upper (respectively, lower) triangular (see (0.9.3)), then $C _ { r } ( \Delta )$ is upper (respectively, lower) triangular; its main diagonal entries are the $\binom { n } { r }$ possible products of r entries chosen from the list $d _ { 1 1 } , \ldots , d _ { n n }$  , that is, they are the <sup>n</sup> scalars $d _ { i _ { 1 } i _ { 1 } } \cdots d _ { i _ { r } i _ { r } }$ such that $1 \leq i _ { 1 } < \cdots < i _ { r } \leq n$ , arranged lexicographically.  Consequently, if $D = \operatorname { d i a g } ( d _ { 1 } , \dotsc , d _ { n } ) \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is diagonal, then so is $C _ { r } ( D )$ ; its main diagonal entries are the <sup>n</sup> possible products of $r$ entries chosen from the list $d _ { 1 } , \ldots , d _ { n }$ , that is, they are the $\binom { n } { r }$ scalars $d _ { i _ { 1 } } \cdot \cdot \cdot d _ { i _ { r } }$ such that $1 \leq i _ { 1 } < \cdots < i _ { r } \leq n$  arranged lexicographically. See chapter $^ 6$ of (Fiedler, 1986) for a detailed discussion of compound matrices. 

0.8.2 The adjugate and the inverse. If $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ and $n \geq 2$ , the transposed matrix of cofactors of A 

$$
\operatorname{adj} A = \left[ (- 1) ^ {i + j} \det A \left[ \{j \} ^ {c}, \{i \} ^ {c} \right] \right]\tag{0.8.2.0}
$$

is the adjugate of A; it is also called the classical adjoint of A. For example, adj ${ \Bigg [ } a \quad b { \Bigg ] } = { \Bigg [ } { \begin{array} { l l } { d } & { - b } \\ { - c } & { a } \end{array} } { \Bigg ] }$ 

A calculation using the Laplace expansion for the determinant reveals the basic property of the adjugate: 

$$
(\operatorname{adj} A) A = A (\operatorname{adj} A) = (\det A) I\tag{0.8.2.1}
$$

Thus, adj A is nonsingular if A is nonsingular, and det $( \operatorname { a d j } A ) = ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) ^ { n - 1 }$ 

If A is nonsingular, then 

$$
\operatorname{adj} A = (\det A) A ^ {- 1}, \quad \text { that   is }, \quad A ^ {- 1} = (\det A) ^ {- 1} \operatorname{adj} A\tag{0.8.2.2}
$$

For example, $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { c } & { d } \end{array} \right] ^ { - 1 } = ( a d - b c ) ^ { - 1 } \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { d } & { - b } \\ { - c } & { a } \end{array} \right]$ if ad = bc. In particular, adj $\overset { \cdot } { A } ^ { - 1 } ) =$ $A / \operatorname* { d e t } A = ( \operatorname { a d j } A ) ^ { - 1 }$ 

If A is singular and rank $A \leq n - 2$ , then every minor of A of size $n - 1$ is zero, so adj $A = 0$ 

If A is singular and rank $A = n - 1$ , then some minor of A of size $n - 1$ is nonzero, so adj $A \neq 0$ and rank adj $A \geq 1$ . Moreover, some list of $n - 1$ columns of A is linearly independent, so the identity $\left( \operatorname { a d j } A \right) A = \left( \operatorname* { d e t } A \right) I = 0$ ensures that the null space of adj A has dimension at least $n - 1$ and hence rank adj $A \leq 1$ . We conclude that rank adj $A = 1$ . The full-rank factorization $\left( 0 . 4 . 6 ( \mathrm { e } ) \right)$ ensures that adj $\boldsymbol { A } = \alpha x y ^ { T }$ for some nonzero $\alpha \in \mathbf { F }$ and nonzero x, $y \in \mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ that are determined as follows: Compute 

$$
(A x) y ^ {T} = A (\operatorname{adj} A) = 0 = (\operatorname{adj} A) A = x \left(y ^ {T} A\right)
$$

and conclude that $A x = 0$ and $y ^ { T } A = 0$ , that is, x (respectively, y) is determined up to a nonzero scalar factor as a nonzero element of the one-dimensional null space of A (respectively, $A ^ { T } )$ . 

The function A → adj A is continuous on $M _ { n }$ (each entry of adj A is a multinomial in the entries of A) and every matrix in $M _ { n }$ is a limit of nonsingular matrices, so properties of the adjugate can be deduced from continuity and properties of the inverse function. For example, if A, $B \in M _ { n }$ are nonsingular, then adj $\ ( A B ) = ( \operatorname * { d e t } A B ) ( A B ) ^ { - 1 } =$ (det $A ( \operatorname* { d e t } B ) B ^ { - 1 } A ^ { - 1 } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } B ) B ^ { - 1 } ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) A ^ { - 1 } = ( \operatorname { a d j } B ) ( \operatorname { a d j } A )$ . Continuity then ensures that 

$$
\operatorname{adj} (A B) = (\operatorname{adj} B) (\operatorname{adj} A) \text {   for   all   } A, B \in M _ {n}\tag{0.8.2.3}
$$

For any $c \in \mathbf { F }$ and any $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ , ad $( c A ) = c ^ { n - 1 }$ adj A. In particular, adj $\left( c I \right) =$ $c ^ { n - 1 } I$ and adj $0 = 0$ 

If A is nonsingular, then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{adj} (\operatorname{adj} A) = \operatorname{adj} ((\det A) A ^ {- 1}) = (\det A) ^ {n - 1} \operatorname{adj} A ^ {- 1} \\ = (\det A) ^ {n - 1} (A / \det A) = (\det A) ^ {n - 2} A \end{array}
$$

so continuity ensures that 

$$
\operatorname{adj} (\operatorname{adj} A) = (\det A) ^ {n - 2} A \text {   for   all   } A \in M _ {n}\tag{0.8.2.4}
$$

If $A + B$ is nonsingular, then $A ( A + B ) ^ { - 1 } B = B ( A + B ) ^ { - 1 } A$ , so continuity ensures that 

$$
A \operatorname{adj} (A + B) B = B \operatorname{adj} (A + B) A \text {   for   all   } A, B \in M _ {n}\tag{0.8.2.5}
$$

Let A, $B \in M _ { n }$ and suppose that A commutes with B. If A is nonsingular, then $B A ^ { - 1 } = A ^ { - 1 } A B A ^ { - 1 } = A ^ { - 1 } B A A ^ { - 1 } = A ^ { - 1 } B , \mathrm { ~ s o } A ^ { - 1 }$ commutes with B. But $B A ^ { - 1 } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) ^ { - 1 } B$ adj A and $A ^ { - 1 } B = ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) ^ { - 1 } ( \operatorname { a d j } A ) B$ , so adj A commutes with B. Continuity ensures that adj A commutes with B whenever A commutes with B, even if A is singular. 

If $A = [ a _ { i j } ]$ is upper triangular, then adj $A = [ b _ { i j } ]$ is upper triangular and each $\begin{array} { r } { b _ { i i } = \prod _ { j \neq i } a _ { j j } } \end{array}$ ; if A is diagonal, then so is adj A. 

The adjugate is the transpose of the gradient of det A: 

$$
(\operatorname{adj} A) = \left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial a _ {i j}} \det A \right] ^ {T}\tag{0.8.2.6}
$$

If A is nonsingular, it follows from (0.8.2.6) that 

$$
\left[ \frac {\partial}{\partial a _ {i j}} \det A \right] ^ {T} = (\det A) A ^ {- 1}\tag{0.8.2.7}
$$

If $A \in M _ { n } \mathrm { ~ i s ~ }$ nonsingular, then adj $A ^ { T } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ^ { T } ) A ^ { - T } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } A ) A ^ { - T } =$ ((det $A ) A ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { T } = ( \operatorname { a d j } A ) ^ { T }$ . Continuity ensures that 

$$
\operatorname{adj} A ^ {T} = (\operatorname{adj} A) ^ {T} \text {   for   all   } A \in M _ {n} (\mathbf {F})\tag{0.8.2.8}
$$

A similar argument shows that 

$$
\operatorname{adj} A ^ {*} = (\operatorname{adj} A) ^ {*} \text {   for   all   } A \in M _ {n}\tag{0.8.2.9}
$$

Let $A = [ a _ { 1 } \dots a _ { n } ] \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ be partitioned according to its columns and let $b \in \mathbf { F } ^ { n }$ Define 

$$
\left(A \leftarrow_ {i} b\right) = \left[ a _ {1} \dots a _ {i - 1} b a _ {i + 1} \dots a _ {n} \right]
$$

that is, $( A  b )$ denotes the matrix whose ith column is b and whose remaining columns coincide with those of A. Examination of the Laplace expansion (0.3.1.1) of det $\textstyle { \left( A \gets b \right) }$ by minors along column i reveals that it is the ith entry of the vector  (adj A) b, that is, 

$$
\left[ \det \left(A \leftarrow_ {i} b\right) \right] _ {i = 1} ^ {n} = (\operatorname{adj} A) b\tag{0.8.2.10}
$$

Applying this vector identity to each column of $C = [ c _ { 1 } \mathrm { ~ } . . . \mathrm { ~ } c _ { n } ] \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ gives the matrix identity 

$$
\left[ \det \left(A \leftarrow_ {i} c _ {j}\right) \right] _ {i, j = 1} ^ {n} = (\operatorname{adj} A) C\tag{0.8.2.11}
$$

0.8.3 Cramer’s rule. Cramer’s rule is a useful way to present analytically a particular entry of the solution to $A x = b$ when $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ is nonsingular. The identity 

$$
A \left[ \det \left(A \leftarrow_ {i} b\right) \right] _ {i = 1} ^ {n} = A (\operatorname{adj} A) b = (\det A) b
$$

follows from (0.8.2.9). If det $A \neq 0$ , we obtain Cramer’s rule 

$$
x _ {i} = \frac {\det (A \leftarrow_ {i} b)}{\det A}
$$

for the ith entry $x _ { i }$ of the solution vector x. Cramer’s rule also follows directly from multiplicativity of the determinant. The system $A x = b$ may be rewritten as 

$$
A (I \leftarrow_ {i} x) = A \leftarrow_ {i} b
$$

and taking determinants of both sides (using multiplicativity) gives 

$$
(\det A) \det (I \leftarrow_ {i} x) = \det (A \leftarrow_ {i} b)
$$

But det $\boldsymbol { \cdot } \boldsymbol { I } \gets \boldsymbol { x } ) = \boldsymbol { x } _ { i }$ , and the formula follows. 

0.8.4 Minors of the inverse. Jacobi’s identity generalizes the adjugate formula for the inverse of a nonsingular matrix and relates the minors of $A ^ { - 1 }$ to those of $A \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ 

$$
\det A ^ {- 1} \left[ \alpha^ {c}, \beta^ {c} \right] = (- 1) ^ {p (\alpha , \beta)} \frac {\det A [ \beta , \alpha ]}{\det A}\tag{0.8.4.1}
$$

in which $\begin{array} { r } { p ( \alpha , \beta ) = \sum _ { i \in \alpha } i + \sum _ { j \in \beta } j } \end{array}$ . Our universal convention is that det $A [ \emptyset ] = 1$ For principal submatrices, Jacobi’s identity assumes the simple form 

$$
\det A ^ {- 1} \left[ \alpha^ {c} \right] = \frac {\det A [ \alpha ]}{\det A}\tag{0.8.4.2}
$$

0.8.5 Schur complements and determinantal formulae. Let $A = [ a _ { i j } ] \in M _ { n } ( \mathbf { F } )$ be given and suppose that $\alpha \subseteq \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ is an index set such that $A [ \alpha ]$ is nonsingular. An important formula for det A, based on the 2-partition of A using α and $\alpha ^ { c }$ , is 

$$
\det A = \det A [ \alpha ] \det \left(A [ \alpha^ {c} ] - A [ \alpha^ {c}, \alpha ] A [ \alpha ] ^ {- 1} A [ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} ]\right)\tag{0.8.5.1}
$$

which generalizes the familiar formula for the determinant of a 2-by-2 matrix. The special matrix 

$$
A / A [ \alpha ] = A [ \alpha^ {c} ] - A [ \alpha^ {c}, \alpha ] A [ \alpha ] ^ {- 1} A [ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} ]\tag{0.8.5.2}
$$

which also appears in the partitioned form for the inverse in (0.7.3.1), is called the Schur complement of A [α] in A. When convenient, we take $\alpha = \{ 1 , \ldots , k \}$ and write A as a 2-by-2 block matrix $A = [ A _ { i j } ]$ with $A _ { 1 1 } = A [ \alpha ] , A _ { 2 2 } = A [ \alpha ^ { c } ] , A _ { 1 2 } = A [ \alpha , \alpha ^ { c } ]$ , and $A _ { 2 1 } = A [ \alpha ^ { c } , \alpha ]$ . The formula (0.8.5.1) may be verified by computing the determinant of both sides of the identity 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left[ \begin{array}{c c} I & 0 \\ - A _ {2 1} A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} & I \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} & A _ {1 2} \\ A _ {2 1} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right] \left[ \begin{array}{c c} I & - A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2} \\ 0 & I \end{array} \right] \\ = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} & 0 \\ 0 & A _ {2 2} - A _ {2 1} A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2} \end{array} \right] \end{array}\tag{0.8.5.3}
$$

which contains a wealth of information about the Schur complement ${ \cal { S } } = [ { s _ { i j } } ] =$ $A / A _ { 1 1 } = A _ { 2 2 } - A _ { 2 1 } A _ { 1 1 } ^ { - 1 } A _ { 1 2 } \mathrm { ; }$ 

(a) The Schur complement S arises (uniquely) in the lower right corner if linear combinations of the first k rows (respectively, columns) of A are added to the last $n - k$ rows (respectively, columns) in such a way as to produce a zero block in the lower left (respectively, upper right) corner; this is block Gaussian elimination, and it is (uniquely) possible because $A _ { 1 1 }$ is nonsingular. Any submatrix of A that includes $A _ { 1 1 }$ as a principal submatrix has the same determinant before and after the block eliminations that produce the block diagonal form in (0.8.5.3). Thus, for any index set $\beta = \{ i _ { 1 } , \dots , i _ { m } \} \subseteq \{ 1 , \dots , n - k \}$ , if we construct the shifted index set $\tilde { \beta } = \{ i _ { 1 } + k , \dots , i _ { m } + k \}$ , then det $A [ \alpha \cup \tilde { \beta } , \alpha \cup \tilde { \gamma } ]$ (before) $= \operatorname* { d e t } ( A _ { 1 1 } \oplus S [ \beta , \gamma ] )$ (after), so 

$$
\det S [ \beta , \gamma ] = \det A [ \alpha \cup \tilde {\beta}, \alpha \cup \tilde {\gamma} ] / \det A [ \alpha ]\tag{0.8.5.4}
$$

For example, if $\beta = \{ i \}$ and $\gamma = \{ j \}$ , then with $\alpha = \{ 1 , \ldots , k \}$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \det S [ \beta , \gamma ] & = s _ {i j} \\ & = \det A [ \{1, \dots k, k + i \}, \{1, \dots , k, k + j \} ] / \det A _ {1 1} \end{array} \tag {0}\tag{0.8.5.5}
$$

so all the entries of S are ratios of minors of A. 

(b) rank A = rank A<sub>11</sub> + rank $S \geq \mathrm { r a n k } A _ { 1 1 }$ , and rank $A = \operatorname { r a n k } A _ { 1 1 }$ if and only if $A _ { 2 2 } = A _ { 2 1 } A _ { 1 1 } ^ { - 1 } A _ { 1 2 }$ 

(c) A is nonsingular if and only if S is nonsingular, since det $A = \operatorname* { d e t } A _ { 1 1 }$ det S. If A is nonsingular, then det $S = \operatorname* { d e t } A / \operatorname* { d e t } A _ { 1 1 }$ 

Suppose that A is nonsingular. Then inverting both sides of (0.8.5.3) gives a presentation of the inverse different from that in (0.7.3.1): 

$$
A ^ {- 1} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} A _ {1 1} + A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2} S ^ {- 1} A _ {2 1} A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} & - A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} A _ {1 2} S ^ {- 1} \\ - S ^ {- 1} A _ {2 1} A _ {1 1} ^ {- 1} & S ^ {- 1} \end{array} \right]\tag{0.8.5.6}
$$

Among other things, this tells us that $A ^ { - 1 } [ \{ k + 1 , \ldots , n \} ] = S ^ { - 1 }$ , so 

$$
\det A ^ {- 1} \left[ \{k + 1, \dots , n \} \right] = \det A _ {1 1} / \det A\tag{0.8.5.7}
$$

This is a form of Jacobi’s identity (0.8.4.1). Another form results from using the adjugate to write the inverse, which gives 

$$
\det \left((\operatorname{adj} A) [ \{k + 1, \dots , n \} ]\right) = (\det A) ^ {n - k - 1} \det A _ {1 1}\tag{0.8.5.8}
$$

When $\alpha ^ { c }$ consists of a single element, the Schur complement of A[α] in A is a scalar and (0.8.5.1) reduces to the identity 

$$
\det A = A \left[ \alpha^ {c} \right] \det A [ \alpha ] - A \left[ \alpha^ {c}, \alpha \right] (\operatorname{adj} A [ \alpha ]) A \left[ \alpha , \alpha^ {c} \right]\tag{0.8.5.9}
$$

which is valid even if $A [ \alpha ]$ is singular. For example, if $\alpha = \{ 1 , \ldots , n - 1 \}$ , then $\alpha ^ { c } = \{ n \}$ and A is presented as a bordered matrix 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \tilde {A} & x \\ y ^ {T} & a \end{array} \right]
$$

with $a \in \mathbf { F } , x , y \in \mathbf { F } ^ { n - 1 }$ , and $\tilde { A } \in M _ { n - 1 } ( { \bf F } ) ; ( 0 . 8 . 5 . 9 )$ is the Cauchy expansion of the determinant of a bordered matrix 

$$
\det \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \tilde {A} & x \\ y ^ {T} & a \end{array} \right] = a \det \tilde {A} - y ^ {T} (\operatorname{adj} \tilde {A}) x\tag{0.8.5.10}
$$

The Cauchy expansion (0.8.5.10) involves signed minors of A of size $n - 2$ (the entries of adj A<sup>˜</sup>) and a bilinear form in the entries of a row and column; the Laplace expansion (0.3.1.1) involves signed minors of A of size $n - 1$ and a linear form in the entries of a row or column. If $a \neq 0$ , we can use the Schur complement of [a] in A to express 

$$
\det \left[ \begin{array}{c c} \tilde {A} & x \\ y ^ {T} & a \end{array} \right] = a \det (\tilde {A} - a ^ {- 1} x y ^ {T})
$$

Equating the right-hand side of this identity to that of (0.8.5.10) and setting $a = - 1$ gives Cauchy’sformulafor the determinant ofa rank-one perturbation 

$$
\det \left(\tilde {A} + x y ^ {T}\right) = \det \tilde {A} + y ^ {T} (\operatorname{adj} \tilde {A}) x\tag{0.8.5.11}
$$

The uniqueness property of the Schur complement discussed in (a) can be used to derive an identity involving a Schur complement within a Schur complement. Suppose that the nonsingular k-by-k block $A _ { 1 1 }$ is partitioned as a 2-by-2 block matrix $A _ { 1 1 } =$ $[ \mathcal { A } _ { i j } ]$ in which the upper left -by- block $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 1 1 }$ is nonsingular. Write $A _ { 2 1 } = [ A _ { 1 } \ A _ { 2 } ]$ in which $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 1 }$ is $( n - k ) – \mathbf { b y }  – \ell$ , and write $A _ { 1 2 } ^ { T } = [ B _ { 1 } ^ { T } ~ B _ { 2 } ^ { T } ]$ , in which $\boldsymbol { B } _ { 1 }$ is $\ell { \ - } \mathbf { b y } { - } ( n - k )$ this gives the refined partition 

$$
A = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} \mathcal {A} _ {1 1} & \mathcal {A} _ {1 2} & \mathcal {B} _ {1} \\ \mathcal {A} _ {2 1} & \mathcal {A} _ {2 2} & \mathcal {B} _ {2} \\ \mathcal {A} _ {1} & \mathcal {A} _ {2} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

Now add linear combinations of the first  rows of A to the next $k - \ell$ rows to reduce $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 2 1 }$ to a zero block. The result is 

$$
A ^ {\prime} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} \mathcal {A} _ {1 1} & \mathcal {A} _ {1 2} & \mathcal {B} _ {1} \\ 0 & A _ {1 1} / \mathcal {A} _ {1 1} & \mathcal {B} _ {2} ^ {\prime} \\ \mathcal {A} _ {1} & \mathcal {A} _ {2} & A _ {2 2} \end{array} \right]
$$

in which we have identified the resulting 2,2 block of $A ^ { \prime }$ as the (necessarily nonsingular) Schur complement of $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 1 1 }$ in $A _ { 1 1 }$ . Now add linear combinations of the first k rows of 

$A ^ { \prime }$ to the last $n - k$ rows to reduce $[ A _ { 1 } \ A _ { 2 } ]$ to a zero block. The result is

A ^ {\prime \prime} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c} \mathcal {A} _ {1 1} & \mathcal {A} _ {1 2} & \mathcal {B} _ {1} \\ 0 & A _ {1 1} / \mathcal {A} _ {1 1} & \mathcal {B} _ {2} ^ {\prime} \\ 0 & 0 & A / A _ {1 1} \end{array} \right]
$$

in which we have identified the resulting 3,3 block of $A ^ { \prime \prime }$ as the Schur complement of $A _ { 1 1 }$ in $A$ . The lower right 2-by-2 block of $A ^ { \prime \prime }$ must be $A / A _ { 1 1 }$ , the Schur complement of $\boldsymbol { A } _ { 1 1 }$ in A. Moreover, the lower right block of $A / A _ { 1 1 }$ must be the Schur complement of $A _ { 1 1 } / \mathcal { A } _ { 1 1 }$ in $A / A _ { 1 1 }$ . This observation is the quotient property ofSchur complements:

If the four blocks $A _ { i j }$ in (0.8.5.3) are square and the same size, and if $A _ { 1 1 }$ commutes with $A _ { 2 1 }$ , then
