Politi, Explicit polar decompositions of complex matrices, Electron. J. Linear Algebra 18 (2009) 693–699. 

## 7.4 Consequences of the polar and singular value decompositions

The polar and the singular value decompositions appear in a host of interesting matrix analytic problems. We sample several of them in this section; more are presented in the problems. Throughout this section, if $X \in M _ { m , n }$ , we let $q = \min \{ m , n \}$ and denote its nonincreasingly ordered singular values by $\sigma _ { 1 } ( X ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( X )$ . The matrix $\Sigma ( X ) =$ $\left[ s _ { i j } \right]$ is the m-by-n diagonal matrix such that $s _ { i i } = \sigma _ { i } ( X )$ for each $i = 1 , \ldots , q$ 

7.4.1 von Neumann’s trace theorem. The following singular value inequality plays a key role in many matrix approximation problems. Our proof of the core inequality is in (8.7), where we obtain it as an application of Birkhoff’s theorem. 

Theorem 7.4.1.1 (von Neumann). Let A, $B \in M _ { m , n }$ , let $q = \min \{ m , n \}$ , and let $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A )$ and $\sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) \ge \cdots \ge \sigma _ { q } ( B )$ denote the non-increasingly ordered singular values of A and B, respectively. Then 

$$
\operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A B ^ {*}) \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (B)\tag{7.4.1.2}
$$

Proof. If $m = n$ , the stated inequality is exactly the assertion of (8.7.6). If $m > n ,$ augment A and B with a block of zeroes to obtain square matrices, that is, define $ { \mathcal { A } } = [ A 0 ] ,  { \mathcal { B } } = [ B 0 ] \in M _ { m }$ . Then $\mathcal { A } B ^ { \ast } = A B ^ { \ast }$ , so it follows from (8.7.6) that $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { R e } \operatorname { t r } ( A B ^ { * } ) = \mathrm { R e } \operatorname { t r } ( A B ^ { * } ) \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) \sigma _ { i } ( B ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) \sigma _ { i } ( B ) } \end{array}$ . If $m < n$ , define $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { A } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { A } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] , \mathcal { B } = \left[ \begin{array} { c } { B } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] \in M _ { n } } \end{array}$ . Then $\boldsymbol { \mathcal { A B ^ { * } } } = \left\lceil \begin{array} { c c } { \boldsymbol { A B ^ { * } } } & { \boldsymbol { 0 } } \\ { \boldsymbol { 0 } } & { \boldsymbol { 0 } } \end{array} \right\rceil$ , so it follows from (8.7.6) again that $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { R e } \operatorname { t r } ( \bar { \dot { A } } \bar { \dot { B ^ { * } } } ) = \mathrm { R e } \bar { \operatorname { t r } ( \dot { A } \dot { B ^ { * } } ) } \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sigma _ { i } ( \dot { A } ) \bar { \sigma _ { i } } ( \dot { B } ) \bar { = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) } \sigma _ { i } ( B ) . } \end{array}$  

Corollary 7.4.1.3. Let A, $B \in M _ { m , n } , l e t q = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ m , n \}$ , and let $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A )$ and $\sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) \ge \cdots \ge \sigma _ { q } ( B )$ ) denote the nonincreasingly ordered singular values ofA and B, respectively. Then 

$$
(a) \| A - B \| _ {2} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2}
$$

$$
(b) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) = \left\{ \begin{array}{c} \max _ {\text {unitary} U \in M _ {n}} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A U) i f m \leq n \\ \max _ {\text {unitary} U \in M _ {m}} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (U A) i f m \geq n \end{array} \right.
$$

$$
(c) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (\bar {B}) = \max \{\operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A T B ^ {*} U): T \in M _ {n} a n d U \in M _ {m} a r e u n i t a r y \}
$$

$$
(d) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A B ^ {*}) \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (B)
$$

Proof. (a) Use the Frobenius inner product and (7.4.1.2) to compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| A - B \| _ {2} ^ {2} = \langle A - B, A - B \rangle_ {F} \\ \qquad = \langle A, A \rangle_ {F} - \langle A, B \rangle_ {F} - \langle B, A \rangle_ {F} + \langle B, B \rangle_ {F} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) - 2 \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A B ^ {*}) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (B) \\ \qquad \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) - 2 \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (B) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (B) \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2} \end{array}
$$

(b) If $m \leq n$ , let $\mathcal { A } = \left[ \begin{array} { l } { A } \\ { 0 } \end{array} \right] \in M _ { n }$ and use (7.4.1.2): 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A U) = \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} \mathcal {A} U \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sigma_ {i} (\mathcal {A}) \sigma_ {i} (U ^ {*}) \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sigma_ {i} (\mathcal {A}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \end{array}
$$

If $A = P U$ is a polar factorization, then $\mathrm { R e } \operatorname { t r } ( A U ^ { * } ) = \mathrm { R e }$ tr $\textstyle P = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A )$ , so the upper bound can be achieved. If $m \geq n$ , let $\mathcal { A } = \left[ A \ 0 \right] \in M _ { m }$ and use $( 7 . 4 . 1 . 2 ) $ again: 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (U A) & = \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} U \mathcal {A} \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {i} (U) \sigma_ {i} (\mathcal {A} ^ {*}) \\ & = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {i} (\mathcal {A}) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \end{array}
$$

If $A = U Q$ is a polar factorization, then Re $\textstyle \mathrm { t r } ( U ^ { * } A ) = \operatorname { R e } \operatorname { t r } Q = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A )$ , so the upper bound can be achieved. 

(c) Use (7.4.1.2) to compute Re tr(AT $\begin{array} { r } { B ^ { * } U ) \le \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A T ) \sigma _ { i } ( U ^ { * } B ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) } \end{array}$ $\sigma _ { i } ( B )$ for any unitary T and U. If $A = V _ { 1 } \Sigma _ { 1 } W _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ and $B = V _ { 2 } \Sigma _ { 2 } W _ { 2 } ^ { * }$ are singular value decompositions in which the diagonal entries of $\Sigma _ { 1 }$ and $\Sigma _ { 2 }$ are, respectively, $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A )$ and $\sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) \ge \cdots \ge \sigma _ { q } ( B )$ , then the upper bound is achieved for $T = W _ { 1 } W _ { 2 } ^ { * }$ and $U = V _ { 2 } V _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ ; with these choices, $A T B ^ { * } U = V _ { 1 } \Sigma _ { 1 } \Sigma _ { 2 } ^ { T } V _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ , whose trace is $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) \sigma _ { i } ( B )$ 

(d) Let $A B ^ { * } = P U$ be a polar decomposition. Use (7.4.1.2) to compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A B ^ {*}) = \operatorname{tr} P = \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A B ^ {*} U) \\ \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (U ^ {*} B) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (B) \end{array}
$$

Part (b) of the preceding corollary ensures that Re tr $\begin{array} { r } { A \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) } \end{array}$ for any $A \in$ $M _ { m , n }$ , but for some applications it is important to identify the case of equality. For example, if A is square, the following theorem shows that Re tr $\begin{array} { r } { A = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) } \end{array}$ if and only if A is positive semidefinite. 

Theorem 7.4.1.4. Let $A = [ a _ { i j } ] \in M _ { m , n }$ , let $q = \min \{ m , n \}$ and $p = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ m , n \}$ , let $\alpha = \{ 1 , \ldots , q \}$ , and let $\sigma _ { 1 } \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q }$ be the nonincreasingly ordered singular values ofA. Then Re tr $\textstyle A \leq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i }$ , with equality ifand only ifthe leading principal submatrix A[α] is positive semidefinite and A has no nonzero entries outside this principal submatrix. 

Proof. We are concerned only with the case ofequality. To prove that the asserted conditions are sufficient, observe that if the principal submatrix $A [ \alpha ]$ is positive semidefinite, then its eigenvalues are its singular values, which are also the singular values of A since no other entries of A are nonzero; the trace of $A [ \alpha ]$ is the sum of its eigenvalues, which is the sum of the singular values of A. 

Now suppose that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname { R e } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } a _ { i i } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i \cdot } \operatorname { I f } \ A = 0 } \end{array}$ there is nothing to prove, so let rank $A = r \geq 1$ . If necessary, augment A with zero blocks to obtain a square matrix $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { A } = \left\lceil \begin{array} { l l } { A } & { 0 _ { m , p - n } } \\ { 0 _ { p - m , n } } & { 0 _ { p - m , p - n } } \end{array} \right\rceil \in M _ { p } } \end{array}$ , which has the same trace and singular values as A. Let $\mathcal { A } = \bar { V } \Sigma _ { r } W ^ { * }$ be a thin singular value decomposition (7.3.2a), in which $V =$ $[ v _ { 1 } ~ \ldots ~ v _ { r } ] \in M _ { p , r }$ and $W = [ w _ { 1 } \dots w _ { r } ] \in M _ { p , r }$ have orthonormal columns, and $\Sigma _ { r } = \operatorname { d i a g } ( \sigma _ { 1 } , . . . , \sigma _ { r } )$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} \mathcal {A} & = \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} A = \operatorname{Re} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} a _ {i i} = \operatorname{Re} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {p} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {r} v _ {i k} \sigma_ {k} \bar {w} _ {i k} \\ & = \operatorname{Re} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {r} \sigma_ {k} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {p} v _ {i k} \bar {w} _ {i k} \\ & = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {r} \sigma_ {k} \operatorname{Re} (w _ {k} ^ {*} v _ {k}) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {r} \sigma_ {k} = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {k} \end{array}
$$

It follows that $\mathrm { R e } ( w _ { k } ^ { * } v _ { k } ) = 1$ for each $k = 1 , \ldots , r$ . Since 

$$
1 = \mathrm{Re} (w _ {k} ^ {*} v _ {k}) \stackrel {(\gamma)} {\leq} | w _ {k} ^ {*} v _ {k} | \stackrel {(\delta)} {\leq} \| v _ {k} \| _ {2} ^ {2} \| w _ {k} \| _ {2} ^ {2} = 1
$$

equality at (δ) and the equality case of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ensure that there are scalars $d _ { k }$ such that $v _ { k } = d _ { k } w _ { k }$ for each $k = 1 , \ldots , r ;$ equality at $( \gamma )$ ensures that each $d _ { k } = 1$ . Therefore, $V = W$ and $\mathcal { A } = V \Sigma _ { r } V ^ { * }$ is positive semidefinite. It follows that its principal submatrix $A [ \alpha ]$ is positive semidefinite (7.1.2) and no other entries of A (and hence of A) are nonzero (7.1.10).  

Corollary 7.4.1.5. Let A, $B \in M _ { m , n } , l e t q = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ m , n \}$ , and let $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A )$ and $\sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) \ge \cdots \ge \sigma _ { q } ( B )$ ) denote the nonincreasingly ordered singular values ofA and B, respectively. Then 

(a) $\begin{array} { r } { \| A - B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \geq \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } ( \sigma _ { i } ( A ) - \sigma _ { i } ( B ) ) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , with equality if and only $i f \operatorname { R e } \operatorname { t r } ( A B ^ { * } ) =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) \sigma _ { i } ( B )$ 

(b) If $\begin{array} { r } { \| A - B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } ( \sigma _ { i } ( A ) - \sigma _ { i } ( B ) ) ^ { 2 } } \end{array}$ , then both $A B ^ { * }$ and $B ^ { * } A$ are positive semidefinite, so $\operatorname { t r } ( A B ^ { * } )$ is real and nonnegative 

Proof. (a) The stated inequality is (7.4.1.3a), so we are concerned only with the case of equality, which occurs if and only if the one inequality in the proof of (7.4.1.3a) is an equality, that is, if and only if Re tr( $\begin{array} { r } { A B ^ { * } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) \sigma _ { i } ( B ) } \end{array}$ 

(b) If $\textstyle \| A - B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } ( \sigma _ { i } ( A ) - \sigma _ { i } ( B ) ) ^ { 2 }$ , the preceding theorem and (7.4.1.3d) ensure that 

$$
\operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A B ^ {*}) \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A B ^ {*}) \leq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (B) = \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A B ^ {*})
$$

so Re $\textstyle \operatorname { t r } ( A B ^ { * } ) = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ( A B ^ { * } )$ , and the preceding theorem ensures that $A B ^ { * }$ is positive semidefinite. Since $\lVert A - B \rVert _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \lVert B ^ { * } - A ^ { * } \rVert _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ , it follows that $B ^ { * } ( A ^ { * } ) ^ { * } = B ^ { * } A$ is also positive semidefinite.  

7.4.2 A nearest singular matrix and a nearest rank-k matrix. Every matrix that is sufficiently close to a nonsingular matrix A (with respect to some norm) is nonsingular (see the exercise preceding (5.6.17)), but what can we say about the distance from A to the closed set of singular matrices? How can we identify a nearest singular matrix? Is it unique? 

Let $A = V \Sigma W ^ { * } \in M _ { n }$ be a singular value decomposition in which $\Sigma =$ dia $\mathfrak { g } ( \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) , \ldots , \sigma _ { n } ( A ) )$ and $\sigma _ { n } ( A ) > 0$ . If $B \in M _ { n }$ is singular, then $\sigma _ { n } ( B ) = 0$ . The inequality (7.4.1.3a) ensures that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| A - B \| _ {2} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n - 1} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2} + \sigma_ {n} ^ {2} (A) \geq \sigma_ {n} ^ {2} (A) \end{array}
$$

for every singular $B \in M _ { n }$ , so any B such that $\| A - B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \sigma _ { n } ^ { 2 } ( A )$ is a closest singular matrix to A in the Frobenius norm. The singular values of such a matrix are uniquely determined: they must be the $n - 1$ largest singular values of A and one zero. If we let $\Sigma _ { 0 } = \mathrm { d i a g } ( \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) , \ldots , \sigma _ { n - 1 } ( A ) , 0 )$ and take $\boldsymbol { B } _ { 0 } = V \Sigma _ { 0 } \boldsymbol { W } ^ { * }$ , then $\| A - B _ { 0 } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } ( \sigma _ { i } ( A ) - \sigma _ { i } ( B ) ) ^ { 2 } = \sigma _ { n } ^ { 2 } ( A ) } \end{array}$ and, as predicted by (7.4.1.5), $A B _ { 0 } ^ { * }$ and $B _ { 0 } ^ { * } A$ are positive semidefinite. The distance in the Frobenius norm from A to $B _ { 0 }$ is $\sigma _ { n } ( A )$ and no singular matrix can be closer, so $\sigma _ { n } ( A )$ is the distance in the Frobenius norm from A to the closed set of singular matrices. We may think of $B _ { 0 }$ as a best singular approximation to A in the Frobenius norm. 

What about uniqueness? If $\sigma _ { n - 1 } ( A ) = \sigma _ { n } ( A )$ , let $\hat { \Sigma } _ { 0 } = \operatorname { d i a g } ( \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) , \ldots , \sigma _ { n - 2 } ( A )$ $0 , \sigma _ { n } ( A ) )$ . Then $\boldsymbol { C } _ { 0 } = V \hat { \boldsymbol { \Sigma } } _ { 0 } \boldsymbol { W } ^ { * }$ is singular, $B _ { 0 } \neq C _ { 0 }$ , and $\| A - C _ { 0 } \| _ { 2 } = \sigma _ { n - 1 } ( A ) =$ $\sigma _ { n } ( A ) = \| A - B _ { 0 } \| _ { 2 }$ , so a best singular approximation to A is not unique in this case. If $\sigma _ { n - 1 } ( A ) > \sigma _ { n } ( A )$ , however, then $B _ { 0 }$ is the only singular matrix such that $\| A - B \| _ { 2 } = \sigma _ { n } ( A ) ; \sec { ( 7 . 4 . \mathrm { P } 1 7 ) }$ 

If $A \in M _ { m , n }$ , rank $A = r$ , and $1 \leq k < r$ , the same principles can be employed to find a “best rank-k approximation” to A. Let $A = V \Sigma W ^ { * }$ be a singular value decomposition in which the diagonal entries of $\Sigma \in M _ { m , n }$ are $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A ) )$ . If $B \in M _ { m , n }$ and rank $B = k$ , then (7.4.1.3a) ensures that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| A - B \| _ {2} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2} + \sum_ {i = k + 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) \geq \sum_ {i = k + 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) \end{array}
$$

so any B such that $\begin{array} { r } { \| A - B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { i = k + 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } ( A ) } \end{array}$ is a best rank-k approximation to A. The singular values of such a matrix are again uniquely determined: They must be the k largest singular values of A and $q - k$ zeroes. Ifwe let $\Sigma _ { 0 } \in M _ { m , n }$ be the diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) , \ldots , \sigma _ { k } ( A )$ and $q - k$ zeroes and take $\boldsymbol { B } _ { 0 } = V \Sigma _ { 0 } \boldsymbol { W } ^ { * }$ then $\begin{array} { r } { \| A - B _ { 0 } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \sum _ { i = k + 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } ( A ) } \end{array}$ , so $B _ { 0 }$ is a best rank-k approximation to $A ;$ it is unique if and only if $\sigma _ { k - 1 } ( A ) > \sigma _ { k } ( A )$ . The distance in the Frobenius norm from A to a closest rank k matrix is $( \textstyle \sum _ { i = k + 1 } ^ { q } \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } ( A ) ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ 

7.4.3 Least squares solution of a linear system. Let $A \in M _ { m , n }$ and $b \in \mathbf { C } ^ { m }$ be given, let $m \geq n$ , and suppose that rank $A = k$ . Consider how one might “solve” the linear system $A x = b$ using the singular value decomposition $A = V \Sigma W ^ { * }$ . We want to choose an $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ so that $\| A x - b \| _ { 2 }$ is minimized. Partition $V = [ v _ { 1 } ~ \ldots ~ v _ { m } ] \in$ $M _ { m }$ and $W = [ w _ { 1 } \dots w _ { n } ] \in M _ { n }$ according to their columns. The vector $A x - b =$ $V \Sigma W ^ { * } x - b$ has the same Euclidean norm as the vector $\Sigma W ^ { * } x - V ^ { * } b$ . Let $\xi = W ^ { * } x$ and $\beta = V ^ { * } b$ , so $\xi = [ \xi _ { i } ] = [ w _ { i } ^ { * } x ] _ { i = 1 } ^ { n }$ and $\beta = [ \beta _ { i } ] = [ w _ { i } ^ { * } \beta ] _ { i = 1 } ^ { m }$ . The Euclidean norm of the vector 

$$
\Sigma \xi - \beta = \left[ \begin{array}{c c c c c} \sigma_ {1} \xi_ {1} - \beta_ {1} & \ldots & \sigma_ {k} \xi_ {k} - \beta_ {k} & \beta_ {k + 1} & \ldots & \beta_ {m} \end{array} \right] ^ {T}
$$

achieves its minimum value $\textstyle ( \sum _ { i = k + 1 } ^ { m } | \beta | _ { i } ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ if we choose $\xi _ { i } = \sigma _ { i } ^ { - 1 } \beta _ { i } = \sigma _ { i } ^ { - 1 } w _ { i } ^ { \ast } \beta$ for each $i = 1 , \ldots , k$ ; the Euclidean norm of the vector $\xi$ is minimized if we then choose $\xi _ { i } = 0$ for each $i = k + 1 , \ldots , n$ . That is, $\begin{array} { r } { x = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { k } ( \sigma _ { i } ^ { - 1 } v _ { i } ^ { * } b ) w _ { i } } \end{array}$ is a vector of minimum Euclidean norm such that $\| A x - b \| _ { 2 }$ achieves its minimum value of $\textstyle ( \sum _ { i = k + 1 } ^ { m } | v _ { i } ^ { * } b | ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ 

Exercise. If $A \in M _ { m , n }$ and rank $A = n$ , use the preceding analysis to explain why there is an $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ such that $A x = b$ if and only if b is orthogonal to nullspace $A ^ { * }$ Explain why this solution x is unique and can be expressed as $x = ( A ^ { * } A ) ^ { - 1 } A ^ { * } b$ 

7.4.4 Approximation by a scalar multiple of a unitary matrix. What is the best least squares approximation to a given $A \in M _ { n }$ by a scalar multiple of a unitary matrix? Invoking (7.4.1.3a), for any unitary $U \in M _ { n }$ and any $c \in \mathbf { C } .$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| A - c U \| _ {2} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (c U)) ^ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - | c | \sigma_ {i} (U)) ^ {2} \\ = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - | c |) ^ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) - 2 | c | \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sigma_ {i} (A) + n | c | ^ {2} \end{array}
$$

which is minimized if $\begin{array} { r } { | c | = { \frac { 1 } { n } } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) = \mu } \end{array}$ , the mean of the singular values of A. The resulting lower bound is 

$$
\| A - c U \| _ {2} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} (A) - n \mu^ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \mu) ^ {2}
$$

for any unitary $U \in M _ { n }$ . We know that if $c U$ is a minimizer, then $( c U ) ^ { * } A$ is positive semidefinite. The polar decomposition (7.3.1) suggests that if $A = P U _ { 0 }$ is a polar decomposition, then its unitary polar factor might be a good candidate. We compute tr $\textstyle P = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \sigma _ { i } ( A ) = n \mu$ and 

$$
\begin{array}{r} \| P U _ {0} - \mu U _ {0} \| _ {2} ^ {2} = \| P - \mu I \| _ {2} ^ {2} = \mathrm{tr} P ^ {2} - 2 \mu \mathrm{tr} P + n \mu^ {2} \\ = \| A \| _ {2} ^ {2} - 2 n \mu^ {2} + n \mu^ {2} = \| A \| _ {2} ^ {2} - n \mu^ {2} \end{array}
$$

so $\textstyle { \bigl ( } { \frac { 1 } { n } } \operatorname { t r } P ) U _ { 0 }$ is a best least squares approximation to A by a scalar multiple of a unitary matrix. 

7.4.5 The unitary procrustes problem. Let A, $B \in M _ { m , n }$ . How well can A be approximated in the Frobenius norm by the “rotation” $\because U B$ for some unitary $U \in M _ { m } ?$ This question is known in factor analysis as the unitary Procrustes problemfor A and B. 

For any unitary $U \in M _ { m }$ we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| A - U B \| _ {2} ^ {2} = \| A \| _ {2} ^ {2} - 2 \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A B ^ {*} U ^ {*}) + \| B \| _ {2} ^ {2} \\ \geq \| A \| _ {2} ^ {2} - 2 \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m} \sigma_ {i} (A B ^ {*}) + \| B \| _ {2} ^ {2} \end{array}\tag{7.4.5.1}
$$

with equality if and only if $A B ^ { * } U ^ { * }$ is positive semidefinite. If $A B ^ { * } = P U _ { 0 }$ is a polar decomposition, then $A B ^ { * } U _ { 0 } ^ { * } = P$ is positive semidefinite and $\operatorname { t r } ( A B ^ { * } U _ { 0 } ^ { * } ) = \operatorname { t r } P =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } \sigma _ { i } ( A B ^ { * } )$ , so $\| A - U \bar { B } \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \| A \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } - 2 \operatorname { t r } P + \| B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ achieves the lower bound in (7.4.5.1). 

Thus, $U _ { 0 } B$ is a best least squares approximation to A by a unitary rotation of B and $\| A - U _ { 0 } B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \| A \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } - 2 \operatorname { t r } P + \| B \| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ 

7.4.6 A two-sided rotation problem. Let A, $B \in M _ { m , n }$ . How well can A be approximated in the Frobenius norm by a two-sided rotation U BT for some unitary matrices $U \in M _ { m }$ and $T \in M _ { m } ?$ 

For any such unitary U and T, (7.4.1.3(a)) ensures that 

$$
\| A - U B T \| _ {2} ^ {2} \geq \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (U B T)) ^ {2} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} (\sigma_ {i} (A) - \sigma_ {i} (B)) ^ {2}\tag{7.4.6.1}
$$

Let $A = V _ { 1 } \Sigma _ { 1 } W _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ be a singular value decomposition in which the diagonal entries of $\Sigma _ { 1 }$ are $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A )$ , and let $B = V _ { 2 } \Sigma _ { 2 } W _ { 2 } ^ { * }$ be a singular value decomposition in which the diagonal entries of $\Sigma _ { 2 }$ are $\sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) \ge \cdots \ge \sigma _ { q } ( B )$ . Let $U _ { 0 } = V _ { 1 } V _ { 2 } ^ { * }$ and $T _ { 0 } = W _ { 2 } W _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ . Then $\lVert A - U _ { 0 } B T _ { 0 } \rVert _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \lVert V _ { 1 } \Sigma _ { 1 } W _ { 1 } ^ { * } - V _ { 1 } \Sigma _ { 2 } W _ { 1 } ^ { * } \rVert _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \lVert \Sigma _ { 1 } - \Sigma _ { 2 } \rVert _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } =$ $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } ( \sigma _ { i } ( A ) - \sigma _ { i } ( B ) ) ^ { 2 }$ , so $U _ { 0 } B T _ { 0 }$ achieves the lower bound in (7.4.6.1). 

7.4.7 Unitarily invariant norms and symmetric gauge functions. If $A \in M _ { m , n } .$ if $A = V \Sigma W ^ { * }$ is a singular value decomposition, and if $\| \cdot \|$ is a unitarily invariant norm, then $\| A \| = \| V \Sigma W ^ { * } \| = \| \Sigma \|$ , so a unitarily invariant norm of a matrix depends only on its singular values. What can we say about the nature of that dependence? 

Suppose that $X = [ x _ { i j } ] , Y = [ y _ { i j } ] \in M _ { m , n }$ are diagonal and have diagonal entries $x _ { i i } = x _ { i }$ and $y _ { i i } = y _ { i }$ for $i = 1 , \ldots , q$ . Let $x = [ x _ { i } ] , y = [ y _ { i } ] \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ . Then $X ^ { * } X$ is diagonal and has diagonal entries $| x _ { 1 } | ^ { 2 } , \ldots , | x _ { q } | ^ { 2 }$ (and $n - q$ additional zero entries if $q < n )$ , so the (not necessarily nonincreasingly ordered) singular values of X are $\vert x _ { 1 } \vert , \ldots , \vert x _ { q } \vert$ . Define the function $g : \mathbf { C } ^ { q }  \mathbf { R } ^ { + }$ by 

$$
g (x) = g ([ x _ {1} \ldots x _ {q} ] ^ {T}) = \| X \|
$$

The function g inherits certain properties from the norm $\| \cdot \| :$ 

(a) $g ( x ) \geq 0$ for all $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ since $\| X \|$ is always nonnegative. 

(b) $g ( x ) = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$ since $\| X \| = 0$ if and only if $X = 0$ 

(c) $g ( \alpha x ) = | \alpha | g ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ and all $\alpha \in \mathbf { C }$ since $\| \alpha X \| = | \alpha | \| X \|$ for all $\alpha \in \mathbf { C }$ and all $X \in M _ { m , n }$ 

(d) $g ( x + y ) \leq g ( x ) + g ( y )$ for all $x , y \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ since $\| X + Y \| \leq \| X \| + \| Y \|$ for all $X , Y \in M _ { m , n } .$ 

These four properties ensure that g is a norm on $\mathbf { C } ^ { q } \mathrm { . }$ ; it has two additional properties: 

(e) $g$ is an absolute norm on $\mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ since the matrices X and $\vert X \vert$ associated with the vectors $x = [ x _ { i } ]$ and $\vert x \vert = \left[ \vert x _ { i } \vert \right]$ have the same singular values, namely, $\vert x _ { 1 } \vert , \ldots , \left. x _ { q } \right.$ 

(f) $g ( P x ) = g ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ and every permutation matrix ${ \cal P } \in { \cal M } _ { q }$ since $\| \cdot \|$ is unitarily invariant. For example, if $q = m \leq n$ , then $g ( x ) = \| X \| =$ $\left\| P X ( P ^ { T } \oplus I _ { n - m } ) \right\| = g ( P x )$ 

Exercise. If $q = n \leq m$ , explain why $g ( x ) = g ( P x )$ for all $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ and every permutation matrix $P \in M _ { n }$ 

Exercise. Explain why the Euclidean norm, the max norm, and the sum norm are the vector norms g associated with, respectively, the Frobenius, spectral, and trace norms according to the preceding prescription. Are these norms permutationinvariant absolute norms? 

Definition 7.4.7.1. Afunction $g : \mathbf { C } ^ { q }  \mathbf { R } ^ { + }$ is a symmetric gauge function if it is an absolute vector norm such that $g ( x ) = g ( P x )$ for every $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ and every permutation matrix $P \in M _ { q }$ 

The preceding discussion shows that every unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ determines a symmetric gauge function on $\mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ . The interesting half of the following theorem says that every unitarily invariant norm is determined by a symmetric gauge function, so there is a one-to-one correspondence between unitarily invariant norms on $M _ { m , n }$ and symmetric gauge functions on $\mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ 

Theorem 7.4.7.2. Let m and n be given positive integers and let $q = \min \{ m , n \}$ . For any $A \in M _ { m , n }$ , let $A = V \Sigma ( A ) W ^ { * }$ , in which $V \in M _ { m }$ and $W \in M _ { n }$ are unitary and $\Sigma ( A ) = [ s _ { i j } ] \in M _ { m , n }$ is a nonnegative diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the nonincreasingly ordered singular values of $A \colon \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q } ( A )$ . Let $s ( A ) =$ $[ \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \dots \sigma _ { q } ( A ) ] ^ { T }$ 

(a) $L e t \parallel \cdot \parallel$ be a unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ . For any $x = [ x _ { i } ] \in \mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ , let $X =$ $[ x _ { i j } ] \in M _ { m , n }$ be the diagonal matrix such that $x _ { i i } = x _ { i } f o r$ each $i = 1 , \ldots , q$ . The function $g : \mathbf { C } ^ { q }  \mathbf { R } ^ { + }$ defined by $g ( x ) = \| X \|$ is a symmetric gauge function on $\mathbf { C } ^ { q }$ 

(b) Let g be a symmetric gauge function on C<sup>q</sup> . The function $\| \cdot \| : M _ { m , n } \to \mathbf { R } ^ { + }$ defined by $\| A \| = g ( s ( A ) )$ is a unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ 

Proof. The assertion in (a) has already been proved, so we have only (b) to deal with. First observe that $\| \cdot \|$ is a well-defined function on $M _ { m , n }$ because the singular values of a matrix are uniquely determined. Unitary invariance of the singular values of a matrix ensures that $\| U A V \| = g ( s ( U A V ) ) = g ( s ( A ) ) = \| A \|$ for all unitary $U \in M _ { m }$ and $V \in M _ { n }$ . Because g is a vector norm, we have $\| A \| \geq 0$ for all $A \in M _ { m , n }$ , with equality if and only if $g ( s ( A ) ) = 0$ if and only if $s ( A ) = 0$ if and only if $A = 0$ . Homogeneity follows from observing that $\| c A \| = g ( s ( c A ) = g ( | c | s ( A ) = | c | g ( s ( A ) ) = | c | \| A \|$ 

Finally, we must show that $\| \cdot \|$ satisfies the triangle inequality. For any given $A , B \in M _ { m , n }$ , compute 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| A + B \| = g (s (A + B)) \stackrel {(\alpha)} {=} g ^ {D D} (s (A + B)) \stackrel {(\beta)} {=} \max _ {g ^ {D} (y) = 1} \operatorname{Re} (y ^ {*} s (A + B)) \\ = \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (C)) = 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A + B) \sigma_ {i} (C) \\ \stackrel {(\gamma)} {=} \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \max _ {T, U \text {unitary}} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} ((A + B) T \Sigma^ {*} U) \\ \leq \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \max _ {T, U \text {unitary}} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (A T \Sigma^ {*} U) \\ + \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \max _ {T, U \text {unitary}} \operatorname{Re} \operatorname{tr} (B T \Sigma^ {*} U) \\ \stackrel {(\gamma)} {=} \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) + \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (B) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) \\ = \max _ {g ^ {D} (y) = 1} \operatorname{Re} (y ^ {*} s (A)) + \max _ {g ^ {D} (y) = 1} \operatorname{Re} (y ^ {*} s (B)) \\ \stackrel {(\beta)} {=} g ^ {D D} (s (A)) + g ^ {D D} (s (B)) \stackrel {(\alpha)} {=} g (s (A)) + g (s (B)) \\ = \| A \| + \| B \| \end{array}
$$

We have used (5.5.9(c)) and the hypothesis that g is a norm at the identities labeled (α), (5.5.10) at the identities labeled $( \beta )$ , and $( 7 . 4 . 1 . 3 ( \mathrm { c } ) )$ at the identities labeled $( \gamma )$ We have also made use of (4.3.52) and the fact that the vectors $s ( A + B ) , s ( A )$ , and $s ( B )$ have nonnegative entries, so only y vectors with nonnegative entries need to be considered in achieving the respective maxima.  

A familiar example of a family of symmetric gauge functions on $\mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ is the family of $l _ { p }$ norms (5.2.4). The unitarily invariant norms on $M _ { m , n }$ determined by the $l _ { p }$ norms are known as Schatten p-norms. 

7.4.8 Ky Fan’s dominance theorem. The family of k-norms (5.2.5) are symmetric gauge functions that play a special role in the theory of unitarily invariant norms. The corresponding unitarily invariant norms on $M _ { m , n }$ are known as $K y$ Fan k-norms; we denote them by 

$$
\| A \| _ {[ k ]} = \sigma_ {1} (A) + \dots + \sigma_ {k} (A), \quad k = 1, \dots , q = \min \{m, n \}\tag{7.4.8.1}
$$

Suppose that $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ is a unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ and let $g$ be the symmetric gauge function associated with it, as described in the preceding section, whose notation we adopt. Then, for any $A \in M _ { m , n }$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \| A \| = g (s (A)) = \max _ {g ^ {D} (y) = 1} \operatorname{Re} (y ^ {*} s (A)) \\ = \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) \end{array}\tag{7.4.8.2}
$$

and a summation by parts yields the identity 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) = \sigma_ {1} (\Sigma) \sigma_ {1} (A) + \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {q - 1} \left((\sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) - \sigma_ {i + 1} (\Sigma)) \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {i} \sigma_ {j} (A)\right) \\ \quad + \sigma_ {q} (\Sigma) \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \\ \quad = \sigma_ {1} (\Sigma) \| A \| _ {[ 1 ]} + \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {q - 1} (\sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) - \sigma_ {i + 1} (\Sigma)) \| A \| _ {[ i ]} \\ \quad + \sigma_ {q} (\Sigma) \| A \| _ {[ q ]} \end{array}\tag{7.4.8.3}
$$

Observe that $\sigma _ { 1 } ( \Sigma ) \geq 0$ , each $\sigma _ { i } ( \Sigma ) - \sigma _ { i + 1 } ( \Sigma ) \geq 0$ , and $\sigma _ { q } ( \Sigma ) \geq 0$ , so if $B \in M _ { m , n }$ and $\| A \| _ { [ k ] } \leq \| B \| _ { [ k ] }$ for each $k = 1 , \ldots , q$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) = \sigma_ {1} (\Sigma) \| A \| _ {[ 1 ]} + \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {q - 1} (\sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) - \sigma_ {i + 1} (\Sigma)) \| A \| _ {[ i ]} \\ \qquad + \sigma_ {q} (\Sigma) \| A \| _ {[ q ]} \\ \qquad \leq \sigma_ {1} (\Sigma) \| B \| _ {[ 1 ]} + \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {q - 1} (\sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) - \sigma_ {i + 1} (\Sigma)) \| B \| _ {[ i ]} \\ \qquad + \sigma_ {q} (\Sigma) \| B \| _ {[ q ]} \\ \qquad = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (B) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) \end{array}
$$

Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| A \| = \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (A) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) \\ \leq \max _ {g ^ {D} (s (\Sigma)) = 1} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {q} \sigma_ {i} (B) \sigma_ {i} (\Sigma) = \| B \| \end{array}
$$

This argument shows that if $\| A \| _ { [ k ] } \leq \| B \| _ { [ k ] }$ for each $k = 1 , \ldots , q$ , then $\| A \| \leq \| B \|$ for every unitarily invariant norm ·. Conversely, if $\| A \| \leq \| B \|$ for every unitarily invariant norm $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ on $M _ { m , n }$ , then this inequality must be valid for the Ky Fan k-norms on $M _ { m , n }$ . We summarize these conclusions in the following theorem. 

Theorem 7.4.8.4. Let A, $B \in M _ { m , n }$ be given. Then $\| A \| \leq \| B \|$ for every unitarily invariant norm · on $M _ { m , n } ~ i f$ and only $i f \| A \| _ { [ k ] } \leq \| B \| _ { [ k ] } f o r$ each $k = 1 , \ldots , q =$ min $\{ m , n \}$ 

7.4.9 Approximation bounds for unitarily invariant norms. The inequalities (7.4.1.3(a)) and (7.3.5(b)) say that for the Frobenius norm and any $A , B \in M _ { m , n } .$ $\| A - B \| _ { 2 } \geq \| \Sigma ( A ) - \Sigma ( B ) \| _ { 2 }$ . The inequality (7.3.5(a)) says that for the spectral norm and any $A , B \in M _ { m , n } , \| | A - B \| | _ { 2 } \geq \| | \Sigma ( A ) - \Sigma ( B ) \| | _ { 2 }$ . In fact, these inequalities are valid for every unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ 

Theorem 7.4.9.1. Let m and n be given positive integers and let $q = \min \{ m , n \}$ For any A, $B \in M _ { m , n }$ , let $A = V _ { 1 } \Sigma ( A ) W _ { 1 } ^ { * }$ and $B = V _ { 2 } \Sigma ( B ) W _ { 2 } ^ { * }$ , in which $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } \in$ $M _ { m }$ and $W _ { 1 } , W _ { 2 } \in M _ { n }$ are unitary, and $\Sigma ( A ) = [ s _ { i j } ( A ) ] , \Sigma ( B ) = [ s _ { i j } ( B ) ] \in M _ { m , n }$ are nonnegative diagonal matrices whose diagonal entries $s _ { i i } ( A ) = \sigma _ { i } ( A )$ and $s _ { i i } ( B ) =$ $\sigma _ { i } ( B )$ are the nonincreasingly ordered singular values of A and B, respectively. Then $\| A - B \| \geq \| \Sigma ( A ) - \Sigma ( B ) \|$ for every unitarily invariant norm · on $M _ { m , n }$ 

Proof. Let 

$$
\mathcal {A} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 0 & A \\ A ^ {*} & 0 \end{array} \right] \quad \text {and} \quad \mathcal {B} = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} 0 & B \\ B ^ {*} & 0 \end{array} \right]
$$

According to (7.3.3), the algebraically nonincreasingly ordered eigenvalues of $\mathcal { A }$ are 

$$
\sigma_ {1} (A) \geq \dots \geq \sigma_ {q} (A) \geq \underbrace {0 = \cdots = 0} _ {| m - n |} \geq - \sigma_ {q} (A) \geq \dots \geq - \sigma_ {1} (A)
$$

with similar expressions for the algebraically nonincreasingly ordered eigenvalues of $\boldsymbol { B }$ and $\boldsymbol { A } - \boldsymbol { B }$ . The differences of the respective ordered eigenvalues of $\mathcal { A }$ and $\boldsymbol { B }$ are $\pm ( \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) - \sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) ) , \ldots , \pm ( \sigma _ { q } ( A ) - \sigma _ { q } ( B ) )$ together with $| m - n |$ zeroes. Although it is not clear how to order these values algebraically, the $q$ algebraically largest values are $| \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) - \sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) | , \ldots , | \sigma _ { q } ( A ) - \sigma _ { q } ( B ) |$ |. Theorem 4.3.47(b) ensures that $\lambda ( A - B )$ majorizes $\lambda ^ { \downarrow } ( \mathcal { A } ) - \lambda ^ { \downarrow } ( B )$ , that is, 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \sigma_ {i} (A - B) \geq \max _ {1 \leq i _ {1} <   \dots <   i _ {k} \leq q} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} | \sigma_ {i _ {j}} (A) - \sigma_ {i _ {j}} (B) |, \quad k = 1, \dots , q
$$

Inspection of these inequalities reveals that they are exactly the inequalities 

$$
\left\| A - B \right\| _ {[ k ]} \geq \left\| \Sigma (A) - \Sigma (B) \right\| _ {[ k ]}, \quad k = 1, \dots , q
$$

so $( 7 . 4 . 8 . 4 )$ ensures that $\| A - B \| \geq \| \Sigma ( A ) - \Sigma ( B ) \|$ for every unitarily invariant norm · on $M _ { m , n }$  

One consequence of the preceding theorem is a generalization of the problem of finding a best (in the sense of least squares) rank-k approximation to a given $A \in M _ { m , n }$ with rank $A > k$ , which we considered in (7.4.2). If $\| \cdot \|$ is a unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ and if $B \in M _ { m , n }$ and rank $B = k$ , then $\sigma _ { 1 } ( B ) \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { k } ( B ) > 0 = \sigma _ { k + 1 } ( B ) =$ $\cdots = \sigma _ { q } ( B )$ . Using the fact that a unitarily invariant norm on diagonal matrices in $M _ { m , n }$ is a monotone norm, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \| A - B \| \geq & \| \Sigma (A) - \Sigma (B) \| \\ & = \| \mathrm{diag} (\sigma_ {1} (A) - \sigma_ {1} (B), \dots , \sigma_ {k} (A) - \sigma_ {k} (B), \sigma_ {k + 1} (A), \dots , \sigma_ {q} (A)) \| \\ & \geq \| \mathrm{diag} (0, \dots , 0, \sigma_ {k + 1} (A), \dots , \sigma_ {q} (A)) \| \end{array} \tag {7.4.9}\tag{7.4.9.2}
$$

for any $B \in M _ { m , n }$ such that rank $B = k$ . If $A = V \Sigma ( A ) W ^ { * }$ is a singular value decomposition, we can always attain equality in the inequality (7.4.9.2) with $B =$ $V { \Sigma } _ { 0 } W ^ { * }$ , in which $\Sigma _ { 0 } \in M _ { m , n }$ is a nonnegative diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) , \ldots , \sigma _ { k } ( A )$ , and $q - k$ zeroes. Thus, the same matrix that provides a best rank-k approximation to A in the Frobenius norm provides a best approximation in every unitarily invariant norm. 

Exercise. How closely can $A \in M _ { m , n }$ be approximated in the spectral norm by a rank-k matrix? 

Another consequence of (7.4.9.1) is a version of (6.3.8) (the Hoffman–Wielandt theorem) that is valid for any unitarily invariant norm. For a Hermitian matrix $H \in M _ { n }$ diag $\lambda ^ { \downarrow } ( H ) \in M _ { n }$ is the diagonal matrix whose diagonal entries are the nonincreasingly ordered eigenvalues of H. 

Corollary 7.4.9.3 (Mirsky). Let A, $B \in M _ { n }$ be Hermitian and let $\| \cdot \|$ be a unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { n }$ . Then 

$$
\| \operatorname{diag} \lambda^ {\downarrow} (A) - \operatorname{diag} \lambda^ {\downarrow} (B) \| \leq \| A - B \|\tag{7.4.9.4}
$$

Proof. Let $\mu \in [ 0 , \infty )$ be such that $A + \mu I$ and $B + \mu I$ are both positive semidefinite. Then 

$$
\Sigma (A + \mu I) = \operatorname{diag} \lambda^ {\downarrow} (A + \mu I) = \operatorname{diag} \lambda^ {\downarrow} (A) + \mu I
$$

and $\Sigma ( B + \mu I ) = \mathrm { d i a g } \lambda ^ { \downarrow } ( B ) + \mu I$ . Theorem 7.4.9.1 ensures that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \| \operatorname{diag} \lambda^ {\downarrow} (A) - \operatorname{diag} \lambda^ {\downarrow} (B) \| & = \| (\Sigma (A + \mu I) - \mu I) - (\Sigma (B + \mu I) - \mu I) \| \\ & = \| \Sigma (A + \mu I) - \Sigma (B + \mu I) \| \\ & \leq \| (A + \mu I) - (B + \mu I) \| = \| A - B \| \end{array}
$$

Exercise. Let A, $E \in M _ { n }$ be Hermitian. For which unitarily invariant norms are the bounds in (6.3.4) and (6.3.8) consequences of the preceding corollary? 

7.4.10 Unitarily invariant matrix norms. Let · be a unitarily invariant matrix norm on $M _ { n }$ . For any $A \in M _ { n } , ( 5 . 6 . 3 4 ( \mathrm { d } ) )$ ensures that $\| A \| \geq \sigma _ { 1 } ( A )$ . The following theorem provides a converse to this observation. 

Theorem 7.4.10.1. A unitarily invariant norm $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ on $M _ { n }$ is a matrix norm ifand only $i f \parallel A \parallel \geq \sigma _ { 1 } ( A )$ for all $A \in M _ { n }$ 

Proof. Suppose that $\| X \| \geq \sigma _ { 1 } ( X )$ for all $X \in M _ { n }$ , and let A, $B \in M _ { n }$ be given. We must show that $\| A B \| \leq \| A \| \ \| B \|$ . Let $g$ be the symmetric gauge function determined by ·. In the following computation, we adopt the notation of (7.4.7) and use the fact that g is a monotone norm as well as the singular value inequality $\sigma _ { k } ( A B ) \leq$ $\sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) \sigma _ { k } ( B )$ ; see the exercise preceding (7.3.11): 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \| A B \| = g (s (A B)) = g ([ \sigma_ {1} (A B)   \sigma_ {2} (A B)   \ldots   \sigma_ {n} (A B) ] ^ {T}) \\ \quad \leq g ([ \sigma_ {1} (A) \sigma_ {1} (B)   \sigma_ {1} (A) \sigma_ {2} (B)   \ldots   \sigma_ {1} (A) \sigma_ {n} (B) ] ^ {T}) \\ \quad = \sigma_ {1} (A) g ([ \sigma_ {1} (B)   \sigma_ {2} (B)   \ldots   \sigma_ {n} (B) ] ^ {T}) \\ \quad = \sigma_ {1} (A) g (s (B)) = \sigma_ {1} (A)   \| B \| \\ \quad \leq \| A \|   \| B \| \end{array}
$$

The theorem ensures that the $\mathrm { K y }$ Fan k-norms and the Schatten p-norms for $p \geq 1$ are unitarily invariant matrix norms on $M _ { n }$ 

Although a convex combination of matrix norms need not be a matrix norm (see (5.6.P9)), a convex combination of unitarily invariant matrix norms is always a unitarily invariant matrix norm. 

Corollary 7.4.10.2. Let $\| \cdot \| _ { a }$ and $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { b }$ be unitarily invariant matrix norms on $M _ { n }$ and let $\alpha \in [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Then $\alpha \parallel \cdot \parallel _ { a } + ( 1 - \alpha ) \parallel \cdot \parallel _ { b }$ is a unitarily invariant matrix norm on $M _ { n }$ 

Proof. The convex combination $\alpha \parallel \cdot \parallel _ { a } + ( 1 - \alpha ) \parallel \cdot \parallel _ { b }$ is a unitarily invariant norm, and since 

$$
\alpha \left\| A \right\| _ {a} + (1 - \alpha) \left\| A \right\| _ {b} \geq \alpha \sigma_ {1} (A) + (1 - \alpha) \sigma_ {1} (A) = \sigma_ {1} (A)
$$

the preceding theorem ensures that it is a matrix norm. 

7.4.11 Absolute unitarily invariant norms on matrices. The Frobenius norm of a matrix $A = [ a _ { i j } ] \in M _ { m , n }$ can be expressed as $\| A \| _ { 2 } = ( \sigma _ { 1 } ( A ) ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \sigma _ { n } ( A ) ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ and as $\begin{array} { r } { \| A \| _ { 2 } = ( \sum _ { i , j } | a _ { i j } | ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 } } \end{array}$ , so it is both unitarily invariant and absolute. Are there other absolute unitarily invariant norms on $M _ { m , n } ?$ The following exercise is a first step toward an answer. 

Exercise. Let $\alpha \ge \beta > 0$ be given. Let $\begin{array} { r } { a = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \sqrt { \alpha ^ { 2 } + \beta ^ { 2 } } + \alpha - \beta ) , b = \sqrt { \alpha \beta / 2 } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { c = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \sqrt { \alpha ^ { 2 } + \beta ^ { 2 } } - \alpha + \beta ) } \end{array}$ . Consider the real symmetric matrices $B _ { \pm } =$ $\left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { b } & { \pm c } \end{array} \right]$ . Show that $a , b , c > 0 ;$ ; the eigenvalues of $B _ { + }$ are $\sqrt { \alpha ^ { 2 } + \beta ^ { 2 } }$ and $0 ;$ 

and the eigenvalues of $B _ { - }$ are α and $- \beta$ . Conclude that the singular values of $B _ { + }$ are $\sqrt { \alpha ^ { 2 } + \beta ^ { 2 } }$ and 0, while the singular values of $B _ { - }$ are $\alpha$ and $\beta .$ . Hint: (1.2.4b), $a + c = \sqrt { \alpha ^ { 2 } + \beta ^ { 2 } }$ , and $a - c = \alpha - \beta$ 

Theorem 7.4.11.1. Let · be a unitarily invariant norm on $M _ { m , n }$ . Then $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ is an absolute norm ifand only ifit is a positive scalar multiple ofthe Frobenius norm. 

Proof. For convenience, suppose that $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ is normalized so that $\| E _ { 1 1 } \| = 1$ , in which $E _ { 1 1 } \in M _ { m , n }$ has a 1 in position 1, 1 and zero entries elsewhere. Let $q = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ m , n \}$ and let $\sigma _ { 1 } \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { q }$ denote the singular values of a given $A \in M _ { m , n }$ . We claim that $\| A \| = \| A \| _ { 2 } = ( \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } \dot { + } \cdot \cdot \cdot + \sigma _ { a } ^ { 2 } ) ^ { 1 / 2 }$ 

If rank $A = 1$ , then $\| A \| = { \dot { \| } } \Sigma ( A ) \| = \| \sigma _ { 1 } E _ { 1 1 } \| = \sigma _ { 1 } \| E _ { 1 1 } \| = \sigma _ { 1 } = \| A \| _ { 2 } .$ If rank $A = 2$ , define $A _ { \pm } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { B _ { \pm } } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] \in M _ { m , n } $ , in which $B _ { \pm } = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { b } & { \pm c } \end{array} \right] } , a =$ $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } } + \sigma _ { 1 } - \sigma _ { 2 } ) , b = \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } \sigma _ { 2 } / 2 } . } \end{array}$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { c = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } - \sigma _ { 1 } + \sigma _ { 2 } ) } } \end{array}$ . The preceding exercise ensures that the singular values of $A _ { - }$ are $\sigma _ { 1 } , \sigma _ { 2 }$ , and $q - 2$ zeroes, while the singular values of $A _ { + }$ are $\sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } }$ and $q - 1$ zeroes. In the latter case, rank $A _ { + } = 1$ , so $\| A _ { + } \| = \| A _ { + } \| _ { 2 } = \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = \| A \| _ { 2 } }$ . Since A and $A _ { - }$ have the same singular values and · is unitarily invariant, we have $\| A \| = \| A _ { - } \| ;$ ; since $\left\| \cdot \right\|$ is absolute, we also have $\| A _ { - } \| = \| A _ { + } \|$ . It follows that $\| A \| = \| A _ { - } \| = \| A _ { + } \| = \| A \| _ { 2 }$ 

Proceed by induction on the rank of A. Suppose that rank $A = r \geq 3$ and $\| X \| = \| X \| _ { 2 }$ for every $X \in M _ { n }$ such that rank $X \le r - 1$ . Define $A _ { \pm } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { B _ { \pm } } & { 0 } \\ { 0 } & { 0 } \end{array} \right] \in$ $M _ { m , n }$ , in which $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { \pm } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { b } & { \pm c } \end{array} \right] \oplus \mathrm { d i a g } ( \sigma _ { 2 } , \dots , \sigma _ { r - 1 } ) , a = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { r } ^ { 2 } } + \sigma _ { 1 } - \sigma _ { r } ) } \end{array}$ $b = \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } \sigma _ { r } / 2 }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { c = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( \sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { r } ^ { 2 } - \sigma _ { 1 } + \sigma _ { r } ) } } \end{array}$ . The preceding exercise ensures that the singular values of $A _ { - }$ are $\sigma _ { 1 } , \ldots , \sigma _ { r }$ and $q - r$ zeroes, while the singular values of $A _ { + }$ are $\sqrt { \sigma _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \sigma _ { r } ^ { 2 } } , \sigma _ { 2 } , . . . , \sigma _ { r - 1 }$ , and $q - r + 1$ zeroes. The induction hypothesis ensures that $\lVert A _ { + } \rVert = \lVert A _ { + } \rVert _ { 2 } = \lVert A \rVert _ { 2 }$ ; as in the rank two case, the hypotheses of unitary invariance and absoluteness ensure that $\| A \| = \| A _ { - } \| = \| A _ { + } \| = \| A \| _ { 2 }$ 

If · is not necessarily normalized, we have shown that $\| \cdot \| / \| E _ { 1 1 } \| = \| \cdot \| _ { 2 }$ , that is, $\| A \| = \| E _ { 1 1 } \| \ \| A \| _ { 2 }$ for every $A \in M _ { m , n }$  

Exercise. Use the preceding theorem to give a conceptual proof that the spectral norm on $M _ { n }$ is not an absolute norm if $n \geq 2$ . Compare with (5.6.P40). 

7.4.12 Inequalities of Kantorovich and Wielandt. Let $A \in M _ { n }$ be Hermitian and positive definite; let $\lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\lambda _ { n }$ be its smallest and largest eigenvalues. Our goals are to show that the following two classical inequalities are equivalent and valid and to explore some of their analytic and geometric consequences. 

Kantorovich’s inequality is 

$$
(x ^ {*} A x) (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) \leq \frac {(\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}) ^ {2}}{4 \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n}} \| x \| _ {2} ^ {4} \text {   for   all   } x \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.1}
$$

and Wielandt’s inequality is 

$$
\left| x ^ {*} A y \right| ^ {2} \leq \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {n}}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}}\right) ^ {2} (x ^ {*} A x) (y ^ {*} A y) \text {   for   all   orthogonal   } x, y \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.2}
$$

The inequality (7.4.12.1) is valid if $x = 0$ , and (7.4.12.2) is valid if either $x = 0$ or $y = 0$ , so in the following discussion we consider only the case $x \neq 0 \neq y$ 

Our approach to Kantorovich’s inequality begins with the two positive semidefinite matrices $\lambda _ { n } I - A$ and $A - \lambda _ { 1 } I$ , and the positive definite matrix $A ^ { - 1 }$ . These three Hermitian matrices commute, so their product is Hermitian and positive semidefinite. Therefore, for any nonzero vector $x ,$ we have 

$$
0 \leq x ^ {*} (\lambda_ {n} I - A) (A - \lambda_ {1} I) A ^ {- 1} x = x ^ {*} ((\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}) I - \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n} A ^ {- 1} - A) x
$$

and hence 

$$
x ^ {*} A x + \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n} (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) \leq (\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}) (x ^ {*} x)\tag{7.4.12.3}
$$

Let $t _ { 0 } = \lambda _ { 1 } \lambda _ { n } ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x )$ and rewrite (7.4.12.3) in the equivalent form 

$$
t _ {0} (x ^ {*} A x) \leq t _ {0} (\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}) (x ^ {*} x) - t _ {0} ^ {2}\tag{7.4.12.4}
$$

The function $f ( t ) = t ( \lambda _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { n } ) ( x ^ { * } x ) - t ^ { 2 }$ is concave and has a critical point at $t =$ $( x ^ { * } x ) ( \lambda _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { n } ) / 2$ , where it has a global maximum. Therefore, $f ( t _ { 0 } ) \leq ( x ^ { * } x ) ^ { 2 } ( \lambda _ { 1 } +$ $\lambda _ { n } ) ^ { 2 } / 4$ and it follows from (7.4.12.4) that 

$$
\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n} (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) (x ^ {*} A x) \leq \frac {1}{4} (\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}) ^ {2} (x ^ {*} x) ^ {2}
$$

This is Kantorovich’s inequality (7.4.12.1). 

We claim that Kantorovich’s inequality implies Wielandt’s inequality. Consider a 2-by-2 positive definite matrix $B = { \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { { \bar { b } } } & { c } \end{array} \right] }$ , whose inverse is $B ^ { - 1 } = ( \operatorname* { d e t } B ) ^ { - 1 } \operatorname { a d j } B =$ $\left\lceil \begin{array} { l l } { c / \operatorname* { d e t } B } & { * } \\ { * } & { * } \end{array} \right\rceil$ . Let $\mu _ { 1 } \leq \mu _ { 2 }$ be the eigenvalues of B. With $x = e _ { 1 }$ and $A = B$ , the inequality (7.4.12.1) is 

$$
\frac {(\mu_ {1} + \mu_ {2}) ^ {2}}{4 \mu_ {1} \mu_ {2}} \geq (e _ {1} ^ {*} B e _ {1}) (e ^ {*} B ^ {- 1} e _ {1}) = \frac {a c}{a c - | b | ^ {2}} = \frac {1}{1 - \frac {| b | ^ {2}}{a c}}
$$

and a calculation reveals that 

$$
\frac {| b | ^ {2}}{a c} \leq \left(\frac {\mu_ {1} - \mu_ {2}}{\mu_ {1} + \mu_ {2}}\right) ^ {2} = \left(\frac {1 - \frac {\mu_ {2}}{\mu_ {1}}}{1 + \frac {\mu_ {2}}{\mu_ {1}}}\right) ^ {2}\tag{7.4.12.5}
$$

Now let x and y be any pair of orthonormal vectors in $\mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ and consider the positive definite 2-by-2 matrix 

$$
B = [ x y ] ^ {*} A [ x y ] = \left[ \begin{array}{c c} x ^ {*} A x & x ^ {*} A y \\ y ^ {*} A x & y ^ {*} A y \end{array} \right]
$$

The interlacing inequalities (4.3.38) of the Poincare separation theorem ensure ´ that the eigenvalues $\mu _ { 1 } \leq \mu _ { 2 }$ of B satisfy the inequalities $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } \leq \mu _ { 1 } \leq \mu _ { 2 } \leq$ $\lambda _ { n }$ , so $\begin{array} { r } { 0 < \frac { \mu _ { 2 } } { \mu _ { 1 } } \le \frac { \lambda _ { 2 } } { \lambda _ { 1 } } } \end{array}$ . The inequality (7.4.12.5) and monotonicity of the function $f ( t ) = ( 1 - t ) ^ { 2 } / ( 1 + t ) ^ { 2 }$ on $( 1 , \infty )$ ensure that 

$$
\frac {\left| x ^ {*} A y \right| ^ {2}}{\left(x ^ {*} A x\right) \left(y ^ {*} A y\right)} \leq \left(\frac {1 - \frac {\mu_ {2}}{\mu_ {1}}}{1 + \frac {\mu_ {2}}{\mu_ {1}}}\right) ^ {2} \leq \left(\frac {1 - \frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}}{1 + \frac {\lambda_ {2}}{\lambda_ {1}}}\right) ^ {2} = \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {n}}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}}\right) ^ {2}
$$

This is Wielandt’s inequality (7.4.12.2). 

Exercise. Explain why both (7.4.12.1) and (7.4.12.2) are satisfied if $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ is an eigenvector of A. Hint: The arithmetic–geometric inequality. 

Exercise. If $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ is not an eigenvector of A, explain why $A ^ { - 1 } x -$ $( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) x \neq 0$ and $x - ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) A x \neq 0$ 

Exercise. If $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ is a unit vector, explain why $( x ^ { * } A x ) ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) \geq 1$ , with strict inequality if x is not an eigenvector of A, Hint: $1 = ( x ^ { * } x ) ^ { 2 } = ( x ^ { * } A ^ { 1 / 2 } A ^ { - 1 / 2 } x ) ^ { 2 } \leq$ $\left\| A ^ { \bar { 1 } / 2 } x \right\| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } \left\| A ^ { - 1 / 2 } x \right\| _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } = ( x ^ { * } A x ) ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x )$ , with equality only if $A ^ { 1 / 2 } x =$ $\stackrel { \cdot \cdot } { \alpha } A ^ { - 1 / 2 } \stackrel { \cdot \cdot } { x }$ " ", in which case x is an eigenvector of A. 

To deduce Kantorovich’s inequality from Wielandt’s inequality, let $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ be a unit vector that is not an eigenvector of A, and define $y = A ^ { - 1 } x - ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) x$ . Then $y \neq 0$ and a computation reveals that $x ^ { * } y = 0 , A y = x - ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) A x \neq 0 , x ^ { * } A y =$ $1 - ( x ^ { \ast } A x ) ( x ^ { \ast } A ^ { - 1 } x ) < 0$ , and $y ^ { * } A y = - ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) ( x ^ { * } A y )$ . Wielandt’s inequality in this case is 

$$
(x ^ {*} A y) ^ {2} \leq - \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {n}}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}}\right) ^ {2} (x ^ {*} A x) (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) (x ^ {*} A y)
$$

so we have 

$$
(x ^ {*} A x) (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) - 1 = - x ^ {*} A y \leq \left(\frac {\lambda_ {1} - \lambda_ {n}}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}}\right) ^ {2} (x ^ {*} A x) (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x)
$$

from which it follows that 

$$
(x ^ {*} A x) (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) \leq \frac {(\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}) ^ {2}}{4 \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n}}
$$

This is Kantorovich’s inequality. 

Exercise. Let $u , v \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ be orthonormal vectors such that $A u = \lambda _ { 1 } u$ and $A v =$ $\lambda _ { n } v$ . Let $x = ( u + v ) / \sqrt { 2 }$ and $y = ( u - v ) / \sqrt { 2 }$ . Show that (7.4.12.2) is an equality for the orthonormal vectors x and y, and that (7.4.12.1) is an equality for this unit vector x. 

If $B \in M _ { n }$ is nonsingular with singular values $\sigma _ { 1 } \geq \cdot \cdot \cdot \geq \sigma _ { n } > 0$ , and if we take $A = B ^ { * } B$ in Wielandt’s inequality (7.4.12.2), we obtain the inequality 

$$
| \langle B x, B y \rangle | \leq \left(\frac {\sigma_ {1} ^ {2} - \sigma_ {n} ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {1} ^ {2} + \sigma_ {n} ^ {2}}\right) \| B x \| \| B y \| = \left(\frac {\kappa^ {2} - 1}{\kappa^ {2} + 1}\right) \| B x \| \| B y \|\tag{7.4.12.6}
$$

in which $x , y \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ are orthogonal vectors and $\kappa = \sigma _ { 1 } / \sigma _ { n }$ is the spectral condition number of B. Let $\theta _ { \kappa } \in ( 0 , \pi / 2 ]$ be the unique angle such that cos $\theta _ { k } = ( \kappa ^ { 2 } - 1 ) /$ $( \kappa ^ { 2 } + 1 )$ 

Exercise. Show that sin $\theta _ { \kappa } = 2 \kappa / ( \kappa ^ { 2 } + 1 ) ~ \mathrm { a n d } ~ \cot ( \theta _ { \kappa } / 2 ) = \kappa$ , with $\theta _ { \kappa } \in$ $( 0 , \pi / 2 ]$ 

If B, x, and y are real, then (7.4.12.6) can be written in the form 

$$
\cos \theta_ {B x, B y} = \frac {| \langle B x , B y \rangle |}{\| B x \| \| B y \|} \leq \cos \theta_ {\kappa} \text {   for   all   orthogonal   nonzero   } x, y \in \mathbf {R} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.7}
$$

in which $\theta _ { B x , B y } \in ( 0 , \pi / 2 ]$ is the angle between the real vectors Bx and $B y ;$ see (0.6.3.1). This formulation gives us the geometric inequality $0 \le \theta _ { \kappa } \le \theta _ { B x , B y }$ . Moreover, since there are nonzero orthogonal vectors for which (7.4.12.2) – and hence also (7.4.12.7) – is an equality, we have the geometric interpretation that $\theta _ { k }$ (determined solely by the spectral condition number of $B )$ is the minimum angle between the real vectors Bx and $B y { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } x$ and y range over all orthonormal pairs of real vectors. If κ is large, then $\begin{array} { r } { \frac { \kappa ^ { 2 } - 1 } { \kappa ^ { 2 } + 1 } = \frac { 1 - \kappa ^ { - 2 } } { 1 + \kappa ^ { - 2 } } } \end{array}$ is close to 1 and $\begin{array} { r } { \theta _ { \kappa } = \cos ^ { - 1 } ( \frac { 1 - \kappa ^ { - 2 } } { 1 + \kappa ^ { - 2 } } ) } \end{array}$ is close to zero, and conversely. Thus, κ is large if and only if there is an orthonormal pair of vectors x, y such that Bx and $B y$ are nearly parallel. 

Exercise. Let $B \in M _ { n }$ be nonsingular, let κ be its spectral condition number, and take $A = B ^ { * } B$ in Kantorovich’s inequality. Deduce that 

$$
\left\| B x \right\| _ {2} \left\| B ^ {- *} x \right\| _ {2} \leq \left(\frac {2 \kappa}{\kappa^ {2} + 1}\right) \| x \| _ {2} ^ {2}\tag{7.4.12.8}
$$

and 

$$
\sin \theta_ {\kappa} \| B x \| _ {2} \| B ^ {- *} x \| _ {2} \leq \| x \| _ {2} ^ {2}\tag{7.4.12.9}
$$

for any $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ 

## Problems

7.4.P1 Suppose that $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } \leq \cdot \cdot \cdot \leq \lambda _ { n } , \alpha _ { 1 } , . . . , \alpha _ { n }$ are nonnegative and $\alpha _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + \alpha _ { n } =$ 1. Let $A = ( \lambda _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { n } ) / 2$ and $G = \sqrt { \lambda _ { 1 } \lambda _ { n } }$ (the arithmetic and geometric means of $\lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\lambda _ { n } )$ . Derive the scalar Kantorovich inequality 

$$
\left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \alpha_ {i} \lambda_ {i}\right) \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \alpha_ {i} \lambda_ {i} ^ {- 1}\right) \leq A ^ {2} G ^ {- 2}\tag{7.4.12.10}
$$

from (7.4.12.1). 

7.4.P2 Let $A = [ a _ { i j } ] \in M _ { n }$ be positive definite and have eigenvalues $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } \leq \cdot \cdot \cdot \leq \lambda _ { n }$ We know that $| a _ { i j } | ^ { 2 } < a _ { i i } a _ { j j }$ for all $i \neq j ;$ ; see (7.1.P1). Use (7.4.12.2) to prove the better bound $\begin{array} { r } { | a _ { i j } | ^ { 2 } \leq \left( \frac { \lambda _ { 1 } - \lambda _ { n } } { \lambda _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { n } } \right) ^ { 2 } a _ { i i } a _ { j j } } \end{array}$ for all $i \neq j$ 

7.4.P3 Prove the following 2-matrix generalization of (7.4.12.1): Let $B , C \in M _ { n }$ be commuting positive definite matrices with eigenvalues $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } \leq \cdot \cdot \cdot \leq \lambda _ { n }$ and $0 < \mu _ { 1 } \leq \cdots \leq$ $\mu _ { n } ;$ respectively. The Greub–Rheinboldt inequality says that 

$$
(x ^ {*} B ^ {2} x) (x ^ {*} C ^ {2} x) \leq \frac {\left(\lambda_ {1} \mu_ {1} + \lambda_ {n} \mu_ {n}\right) ^ {2}}{4 \lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n} \mu_ {1} \mu_ {n}} (x ^ {*} B C x) ^ {2}, \quad \text {   any   } x \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.11}
$$

which we can express equivalently as 

$$
\frac {\langle B x , C x \rangle}{\| B x \| _ {2} \| C x \| _ {2}} \geq \frac {2 \sqrt {\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n} \mu_ {1} \mu_ {n}}}{\lambda_ {1} \mu_ {1} + \lambda_ {n} \mu_ {n}}, \quad \text {   any   nonzero   } x \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.12}
$$

Unlike Kantorovich’s inequality, however, if neither B nor C is a scalar matrix, there need not be a unit vector x for which the Greub–Rheinboldt inequality is an equality. (a) Prove (7.4.12.11). (b) Show that equality is possible in (7.4.12.12) if at least one of $B , C$ is a scalar matrix. (c) For what choice of commuting positive definite matrices B and C does (7.4.12.11) reduce to (7.4.12.1)? (d) If B, C, and x are real, interpret (7.4.12.12) geometrically as a lower bound on the cosine of the smaller angle between the vectors $B x$ and $B y$ , that is, as an upper bound on the smaller angle between $B x$ and $B y$ 

7.4.P4 Let $A \in M _ { n }$ be positive definite and have eigenvalues $0 < \lambda _ { 1 } \leq \cdots \leq \lambda _ { n }$ . Let $u _ { 1 } , u _ { n } \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ be orthonormal vectors such that $A u _ { 1 } = \lambda _ { 1 } u _ { 1 }$ and $A u _ { n } = \lambda _ { n } u _ { n }$ , and let $\kappa = \lambda _ { n } / \lambda _ { 1 }$ be the spectral condition number of A. Deduce from (7.4.12.12) that 

$$
\frac {\langle x , A x \rangle}{\| x \| _ {2} \| A x \| _ {2}} \geq \frac {2 \sqrt {\lambda_ {1} \lambda_ {n}}}{\lambda_ {1} + \lambda_ {n}} = \frac {2 \sqrt {\kappa}}{\kappa + 1}, \quad \text {   any   nonzero   } x \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.13}
$$

with equality for the vector $x _ { 0 } = \lambda _ { n } ^ { 1 / 2 } u _ { 1 } + \lambda _ { 1 } ^ { 1 / 2 } u _ { n }$ . If A and x are real, interpret the preceding inequality geometrically: 

$$
\cos \theta_ {x, A x} \geq \frac {2 \sqrt {\kappa}}{\kappa + 1}, \quad \text { any   unit   vector } x \in \mathbf {R} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.14}
$$

in which the lower bound is achieved for the vector $x _ { 0 }$ . Thus, $0 \le \theta _ { x , A x } \le \cos ^ { - 1 } ( 2 \kappa ^ { 1 / 2 } ( \kappa +$ $1 ) ^ { - 1 } )$ for every unit vector x, with equality in the lower bound for every eigenvector of A and equality in the upper bound for $x _ { 0 }$ 

7.4.P5 Let $A \in M _ { n }$ be nonsingular, and let κ be its spectral condition number. Use the polar decomposition and the Kantorovich inequality to show that 

$$
\left| \left(x ^ {*} A x\right) \left(x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x\right) \right| \leq \frac {1}{4} \left(\kappa^ {1 / 2} + \kappa^ {- 1 / 2}\right) ^ {2} \| x \| _ {2} ^ {4}, \quad \text { any } x \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.15}
$$

with equality for some unit vector x. 

7.4.P6 Let κ be the spectral condition number of the positive definite matrix A. Show that the Kantorovich and Wielandt inequalities are, respectively, 

$$
(x ^ {*} A x) (x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x) \leq \frac {1}{4} (\kappa^ {1 / 2} + \kappa^ {- 1 / 2}) ^ {2} \| x \| _ {2} ^ {4}, \quad \text { any } x \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.16}
$$

and 

$$
\left| x ^ {*} A y \right| ^ {2} \leq \left(\frac {\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}\right) ^ {2} (x ^ {*} A x) (y ^ {*} A y), \quad \text { all   orthogonal } x, y \in \mathbf {C} ^ {n}\tag{7.4.12.17}
$$

7.4.P7 Let $A \in M _ { n }$ be nonsingular and Hermitian and have spectral condition number κ. Show that 

$$
\max _ {\| x \| _ {2} = 1} \left(\| A x \| _ {2} \| A ^ {- 1} x \| _ {2}\right) = \frac {1}{2} \left(\kappa + \kappa^ {- 1}\right)
$$

Exhibit a vector x for which the maximum is achieved. 

7.4.P8 Let $A \in M _ { n }$ be positive definite, and suppose that all its eigenvalues lie in the interval $[ m , M ]$ , in which $0 < m < M < \infty$ . Show that $( x ^ { * } A x ) ( x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x ) \leq ( m + M ) ^ { 2 } \left\| x \right\| _ { 2 } ^ { 4 } / 4 m M$ for all $x \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ 

7.4.P9 Let $\alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n } , \beta _ { 1 } , \ldots , \beta _ { n }$ be (not necessarily ordered) positive real numbers. We know that $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \alpha _ { i } \beta _ { i } \le \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \alpha _ { i } ^ { \downarrow } \beta _ { i } ^ { \downarrow } } \end{array}$ ; see (4.3.54). The Kantorovich inequality permits us to reverse this inequality: 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \alpha_ {i} ^ {\downarrow} \beta_ {i} ^ {\downarrow} \leq \frac {m + M}{2 \sqrt {m M}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \alpha_ {i} \beta_ {i}\tag{7.4.12.18}
$$

in which $0 < m \leq \alpha _ { i } / \beta _ { i } \leq M < \infty$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n$ . Provide details: (a) Let $A = \mathrm { d i a g } ( \alpha _ { 1 } / \beta _ { 1 } , \dots , \alpha _ { n } / \beta _ { n } )$ and $x = [ \sqrt { \alpha _ { i } \beta _ { i } } ] _ { i = 1 } ^ { n }$ . Compute $( x ^ { T } A x ) ( x ^ { T } A ^ { - 1 } x )$ and use (7.4.12.1) to provide an upper bound for it. (b) $\begin{array} { r } { ( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \alpha _ { i } ^ { \downarrow } \beta _ { i } ^ { \downarrow } ) ^ { 2 } \leq ( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \alpha _ { i } ^ { 2 } ) ( \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \alpha _ { i } ^ { 2 } ) } \end{array}$ gives a lower bound. 

7.4.P10 Let x, $y \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ be nonzero vectors and let $A , B \in M _ { n }$ be positive definite. (a) Show that $| x ^ { * } y | ^ { 2 } \leq ( x ^ { * } A x ) ( y ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } y )$ , with equality for $x = A ^ { - 1 } y$ . (b) Conclude that the function $f ( A , y ) = ( y ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } y ) ^ { - 1 }$ has the variational representation 

$$
f (A, y) = \min _ {x ^ {*} y \neq 0} \frac {x ^ {*} A x}{| x ^ {*} y | ^ {2}}
$$

(c) Deduce that $f ( A + B , y ) \geq f ( A , y ) + f ( B , y )$ . (d) Let $y = e _ { i }$ , the ith standard unit basis vector, and deduce that $\gamma _ { i i } ^ { - 1 } \geq \alpha _ { i i } ^ { - 1 } + \beta _ { i i } ^ { - 1 }$ , in which $( A + B ) ^ { - 1 } = [ \gamma _ { i j } ] , A ^ { - 1 } = [ \alpha _ { i j } ]$ and $B ^ { - 1 } = [ \beta _ { i j } ]$ . This is Bergstrom’s inequality ¨ . (e) Explain why Bergstrom’s inequality ¨ can be written in the form

\frac {\det (A + B)}{\det (A + B) [ \{i \} ^ {c} ]} \geq \frac {\det A}{\det A [ \{i \} ^ {c} ]} + \frac {\det B}{\det B [ \{i \} ^ {c} ]}, \quad i = 1, \dots , n\tag{7.4.12.19}
$$

in which the denominators are cofactors of main diagonal entries. 

7.4.P11 Let $A \in M _ { n }$ be positive definite, let $x , y \in \mathbf { C } ^ { n }$ , and let $\alpha , \beta$ be real and positive. Let $\begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { A } _ { \alpha } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { A } & { x } \\ { x ^ { * } } & { \alpha } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { B _ { \beta } = \left[ \begin{array} { l l } { B } & { y } \\ { y ^ { * } } & { \beta } \end{array} \right] } \end{array}$ . (a) Show that det $A _ { \alpha } /$ det $A = \alpha - x ^ { * } A ^ { - 1 } x$ det $B _ { \alpha } /$ det $B = \bar { \beta } - y ^ { \bar { * } } B ^ { - 1 } y$ , and $\operatorname* { d e t } ( \bar { \mathcal { A } } _ { \alpha } + \mathcal { B } _ { \alpha } ) / \operatorname* { d e t } ( A + B ) = \alpha + \beta - ( x + y ) ^ { * } ( A +$ $B ) ^ { - 1 } ( x + y )$ ). (b) Show that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {\det (\mathcal {A} _ {\alpha} + \mathcal {B} _ {\alpha})}{\det (A + B)} - \frac {\det \mathcal {A} _ {\alpha}}{\det A} - \frac {\det \mathcal {B} _ {\alpha}}{\det B} \\ = x ^ {*} A ^ {- 1} x + y ^ {*} B ^ {- 1} y - (x + y) ^ {*} (A + B) ^ {- 1} (x + y) \end{array}\tag{7.4.12.20}
$$

(c) Explain why $\mathcal { A } _ { \alpha }$ and $B _ { \beta }$ are positive definite for all sufficiently large positive α, $\beta _ { : }$ , and use (7.4.12.20) to show that (7.4.12.19) implies the Berenstein–Veinstein inequality:

$$

(d) Use (7.4.12.20) to show that (7.4.12.21) implies (7.4.12.19), and conclude that the Bergstrom and Berenstein–Veinstein inequalities are equivalent. ¨
